variants.name: Save Changes to untitled?
variants.angle: This version moves the story from the software and its churches to the grey drawings themselves. The two colours become mute jobs that arrive in tins. The heart is a crew of grey box-head decorators who have only ever worn colour as splashes on their overalls, and who want, just once, to be filled in properly. The religious framing becomes a trade union to avoid real-religion satire. It also fixes the palette arithmetic: black plus 14 greys plus 1 free slot makes 16, so no colour is "already taken" and the blue/yellow pair stays legal.
variants.logline: Inside an unsaved 16-colour picture called untitled live fourteen shades of grey people, and the only colour any of them has ever worn is what splashes on their overalls at work. There is one palette slot left. When the Hand finally clicks Save, whichever colour covers more of the canvas gets it forever, and its decorators finally get coloured in.
variants.world: The world is untitled, a picture open in an unnamed little drawing program that the drawings just call the Program. It has never been saved. Its palette holds 16 colours: black for the lines, fourteen greys for everything else, and Slot 16, which is empty. A hand-lettered sign on Slot 16 says VACANT. ENQUIRE WITHIN. Everything the Hand has drawn is grey: houses with one chimney, a lot of attempted horses, the hill it keeps redrawing, a sun that is a grey circle with grey lines coming out of it because the Hand is waiting to decide. Under every grey is a darker grey, which the drawings call 'the undercoat' and do not talk about. Everything has a black keyline, and the drawings take this very seriously, because a gap in your line is how a Fill gets in, or out. Colour does not live in the world. It turns up in two tins, the left one and the right one, and is only allowed to touch the work and the workers. The world is not sad, just unfinished. It looks like a decorated room before anyone has picked the paint.
variants.the_colours: The colours are mostly mute forces. They do not talk, scheme or have temples. They are jobs. Each match the Hand puts one candidate in the left tin and one in the right, and the drawings sign on with one tin the way a decorator signs on to a contract. All the personality comes from the drawings' gossip about them, which is trade folklore, not character. 'Blue goes on patient; you'll be at it all day.' 'Orange shows every mistake.' 'Pink gets in your cap and you're finding it for weeks.' 'Green dries darker than the tin. Always has.' 'Yellow needs three coats, and they still won't thank you.' Neither colour wants anything we can see. Each just wants to be more of the picture, the way water wants to go downhill. That is the reason the drawings, and not the colours, are the ones with hopes.
variants.the_creator: The Hand is never seen above the wrist and is only ever shown as a crude cursor. It is not a god and not a villain. It is somebody who opened a drawing program a long time ago, drew some people, picked two colours, and keeps getting distracted. It has three habits the drawings know as law. First, it cannot draw hands, so everyone it draws is holding something to hide them. Second, it always starts in the bottom-left corner and gives up halfway. Third, it never names anything, so every file is untitled. The drawings are fond of it the way a crew is fond of a client who pays late but brings biscuits. It appears in person only at the Save, as one slow arrow moving to one hand-drawn button.
variants.who_you_play: You play a grey decorator. Every person in untitled is one, because the Hand cannot draw hands: it drew a roller in the first one's fist to hide the fingers, and once you are holding a roller, what else are you going to be? So the Hand only ever draws one kind of person: a square head, two dots, a line for a mouth, a flat stroke on top that the drawings agree is a cap, and overalls, because overalls are one shape and legs are two. Each decorator is named after their own grey: Putty, Slate, Pewter, Ash, Gravel, Smudge, Concrete, Fog, Ballbearing, Dishwater, Pigeon, Lint, Steel and Old Tooth. Their overalls are coloured only because the paint gets on them at work. That is the only colour any grey has ever worn, and they wear it proudly, like a tan. Each one has a small, specific dream about what they would be if they were filled in properly. Putty wants to find out whether he has freckles. Slate wants red cheeks 'just to see'. Ash has been practising a smile in case the colour makes it look wider. Fog has a feeling her cap was always meant to be a hat. Old Tooth has been grey the longest and says he does not mind, which nobody believes. Lint wants to see what his eyes are, because two dots could be anything.
variants.why_they_fight: A 16-colour file can keep only one more colour, so saving forces the decision. Whichever tin covers more of the canvas when the Hand clicks Save goes into Slot 16 for good, and once a colour is in the palette, the Hand can finally fill people in with it. That is what the decorators are really working for. They are not fighting for the colour. They are fighting to be the crew who gets coloured in: a whole person in one colour, not just splashes on a work uniform. The losing tin's paint goes back to the nearest grey, and so do its decorators' overalls. That is not death. It is just back to how you were, with a bit of a sulk. The crews are not enemies either. They are two firms on the same job, mates in the pub, doing their best to make the other lot's half look patchy. Painting over the other crew is professional rivalry, not hatred, and 'splatting' someone means sending them back to the corner where the Hand starts, to be drawn back in a bit wobblier. Nobody inside can see the score, because you cannot see a picture from inside it. Only the Hand sees the whole canvas, and the Hand does not add up until it saves.
variants.reveal_and_rematch: Reveal: the match freezes mid-stroke. A crude hand-drawn box rolls down over the canvas with the words 'Save changes to untitled?' and three wobbly buttons, then the Hand's arrow drifts toward Yes, very slowly, while every decorator holds their breath and two of them hold hands, with their tools. Click. A progress bar crawls across, filling with chunky pixel blocks as the canvas is counted, and the drawings stand very still because they are being counted too. Then the losing colour dithers to grey one row at a time, top to bottom, like a blind coming down, and its decorators go grey with it, shrugging. The winning colour flies up into Slot 16, the sign changes to OCCUPIED, and the Hand picks up the Fill and does what the winners have been waiting their whole lives for. It clicks inside each winning decorator, one at a time, and the colour pours in like a bath. Putty finds out about the freckles: no freckles, and he is delighted anyway. Rematch: the saved picture goes into a folder the drawings call the Frame, where nobody ever changes again. Then the Hand clicks New, and a fresh untitled opens: one slot free, everything grey. The Hand can only draw one kind of person, so it draws the same crew again, grey, in the corner, holding tools. Nobody quite remembers the last file, but they all have a feeling that somewhere in the Frame there is a coloured one of them, happy forever, and they would like to meet him. The file number ticks up: untitled (2), untitled (3), untitled (48). Tins out.
variants.pairs_explained: The Program has exactly two current-colour tins, the one on the left button and the one on the right, so there are only ever two candidates per job. The Hand has three moods, and each mood reaches for the same two tins every time. Blue/orange is 'the Hand is feeling brave', the classic, and the crews say it is easiest to tell whose wall is whose. Pink/green is 'the Hand has been eating sweets', and both colours stain caps. Blue/yellow is 'the Hand wants a seaside', and blue decorators in this pairing are known to be smug about having been in the other pairing too. Because no colour is already in the palette, every pair is a clean contest, and any colour can win Slot 16 in this file and lose it in the next.
variants.weapons: Every tool is a drawing-program tool that the decorators treat as trade kit, and every tool exists because something has to hide a hand. ROLLER: the Program's widest brush. It is honest work, and the crew respect it most, with the saying 'you can't fake a roller line'. SPRAYER: the spray-can tool, all fizz and speckle. Old hands call it cheating and use it whenever nobody's looking. BUCKET: the Fill. It is the most powerful tool, and the decorators fear it more than anything, because a Fill goes everywhere that is not closed, which is why Rule One of the union is CLOSE YOUR LINES. In world, the bucket leaks through any gap in a line, and box-heads check their own keylines nervously after a big pour. MISTER: the smallest spray nozzle, 'a rumour of colour'. Apprentices are given it on their first day and told it is a promotion. Future tools come from the Program's toolbar, each with a trade spin: the Line tool as a chalk-line snapper, the Rectangle tool as a 'skirting board', the Eraser as a contraband scraper the union has formally banned, and the Pencil, which the crew will not touch because it is how the Hand made them and it feels rude.
arenas: The Corner (Close Quarters): the bottom-left of the canvas, where the Hand always starts drawing and always gives up. It is cramped, half finished and full of abandoned first strokes.
The Hill the Hand Keeps Redoing (King of the Hill): one hill drawn eleven times on top of itself. The crew who holds the top holds the view of the whole job.
Drawn on the Bus (Turbulence): everything here was drawn on a moving vehicle. Lines wobble, platforms lurch and the wind is just the Hand's elbow.
Warm-Up Scribbles (Movement Course): the loops, zigzags and spirals the Hand does to test the pen before drawing anything real. The apprentices train here.
The Attempted Horse: an arena inside the Hand's fourth go at a horse. Nobody is sure which end is which, and both ends have a ramp.
Mid-Undo: platforms flicker in and out while somebody somewhere is holding the undo key.
800%: a job done zoomed in, where every pixel is a block the size of a decorator and a single dot of paint is a wall.
Behind the Box: the strip of canvas the Save box always covers. Nobody has ever painted it, and the crews suspect it is the most important bit.
variants.menus_and_meta: Title: a crude hand-drawn box reads 'Save changes to untitled?'. Yes plays, No goes to options ('no, not yet'), and Cancel quits ('the Hand has gone for a cup of tea'). The box is drawn in the author's own wobble, never a real dialog layout. Team select is the yard: the grey decorators queue at two tins, left and right, and pick one up. Your character card shows their grey number and their one dream ('PUTTY, Grey 7. Would like to know about freckles.'). Loading screen: 'The Hand is thinking.' with the arrow drawing slow circles. Pause: 'The Hand has let go of the mouse.' Results: the Save sequence is the results screen. After it, a little card shows each winner filled in, with their dream answered in one line ('SLATE: cheeks confirmed.'). Progression: the Frame is a gallery of every saved match, the actual final painted canvas thumbnail named untitled (n), so the meta-progression is literally a growing folder of real pictures players made together. Unlocks are new dreams for each grey, new things the Hand attempts to draw (arenas), and new toolbar tools. Some drawings only appear after a certain file number, because the Hand gets a bit better and then worse again. The file counter in the corner, untitled (48), is the session's match count.
variants.escalation: The premise generates content in several directions, so it is not one joke. (1) Fourteen greys, each with a dream. Each dream can be answered on a win and replaced by a new, smaller, stranger one ('Putty, after freckles: wonders if he has knees'), so the cast keeps evolving across files. (2) The Hand's drawing career. New arenas are new things the Hand tries and fails to draw: the horse, a bicycle, 'a crowd', its own hand (a horror level the crew refuse to enter). (3) The union. Local 16, the Amalgamated Society of Grey Decorators, issues rules that turn up as loading tips and form a running gag ('Rule 4: no Fill before tea.' 'Rule 9: if the Hand draws you a second time, you are your own apprentice.'). (4) The Frame. Saved pictures build up, and the drawings keep sending messages toward the coloured versions of themselves, half envious and half proud, with occasional replies that are just a colour swatch. (5) The Program changes. A future update brings tools, a bigger canvas or, the thing they fear most, 256 colours, which would make the whole war pointless and must be stopped. That works as a seasonal story arc. (6) Mixing. A future mode could ask what happens when two tins meet in a gap neither crew closed. Each new idea has to come back to the slot, the tins and the wish to be filled in.
tone_captions: SLOT 16: VACANT. ENQUIRE WITHIN.
LOCAL 16, RULE ONE: CLOSE YOUR LINES.
The Hand cannot draw hands. That is why we all hold something.
Putty has been grey for 11,000 undos. He would just like to try a cheek.
A Fill goes everywhere you aren't closed. Mind your gaps, love.
SAVING... (STAND STILL. YOU ARE BEING COUNTED.)
Somewhere in the Frame there's an orange one of me. I hope he's happy. I hope he's got freckles.
Back to grey. Not gone. Just grey, with a sulk.
untitled (48). Same crew. Grey again. Tins out.
variants.name_options: Game title: Colour Wars still fits, and fits better than before, because it is what the grey drawings call the whole business: two firms on one job, a war fought entirely in colour by people who have none. It can carry a subtitle on the title box, such as 'Colour Wars: Save changes to untitled?', or leave the question as the title screen gag. The file: always 'untitled', numbered by save, untitled (2) and up, which is generic and never a brand. The program: unnamed in world, called 'the Program' by the drawings. If it ever needs a name on screen, use something invented and plain like 'Doodle' or 'Scribble 16', drawn in the author's hand. Never a real product name, logo or icon. The creator: the Hand. The saved archive: the Frame. The union: Local 16, the Amalgamated Society of Grey Decorators. The people: greys, the crew or decorators, each named for their shade (Putty, Slate, Pewter, Ash, Gravel, Smudge, Concrete, Fog, Ballbearing, Dishwater, Pigeon, Lint, Steel, Old Tooth).
variants.risks: 1. Trade dress. The phrase 'Save changes to untitled?' is close to real software prompt text, and two current-colour tins, a 16-colour palette, a spray tool and a Fill will all read as evoking one famous program. It needs discipline: the author's own wobbly drawing only, no real dialog proportions, button order, icons, title bars, cursors or palette grid layout, and no Windows or Microsoft naming anywhere. If legal comfort is wanted, retitle the box ('Keep this one?') and keep the gag. 2. One-joke risk moves rather than vanishing. The Save reveal is the strongest beat and will be seen every match. It needs variation, such as different crawl speeds, the Hand hovering over No, or a rare double-click, or it becomes a skip button. The drawings' dreams carry the long tail, but only if someone keeps writing them. 3. Melancholy. 'Grey people who long for colour' can tip into sad, and the loser dithering to grey can look like dying. The fiction must keep saying that grey is fine, nobody is erased, and the Hand redraws everyone next file. Keep the tone at teatime builders, not tragedy. 4. Narrative cost. This game has no story system. All of this has to land through captions, a results card, loading tips and character cards, and the dreams are the most expensive part (writing for 14 characters). 5. Fourteen named greys versus four seats: players pick a 'character', which suggests distinct art the box-head style deliberately does not have. Distinct greys and caps may be all the variety there is, and Fog and Ash will look identical. 6. Period piece. A 16-colour palette and an unsaved file nod to older software. Keep the software generic and the drawings timeless, so it reads as 'childhood drawing' more than '1998'. 7. Mute colours mean no villain. The rivalry is two friendly crews, which suits a local party game but gives less drama than 'Feed the Hues'. The proposed hybrid's petty colour-gods would cut against this angle. Only the 'never draw well' line could survive, as a union rule, not a commandment. 8. Coherence checks. The world must stay grey: no coloured props, no coloured sun, and the victory fill-in happens only on players. 'You can't see the picture from inside it' explains the hidden score well, but split-screen players can still see the paint near them, so the fiction covers the total, not the local view.

longevity.strongest: It has the most heart and the best painter-tradesman fit. 'The Hand cannot draw hands, so everyone holds a tool' is a superb weird origin. The union, Local 16 (CLOSE YOUR LINES), the Fill-in victory, the Frame as a gallery of real end-of-match canvases, and '256 colours' as a seasonal existential threat are all long-running.
longevity.weakest: The colours are mute, so the two-colour fight for the slot becomes background and the crews' dreams take the centre. That moves away from the core the author praised. The fourteen named greys suggest distinct characters the art style cannot show, and the tone risks melancholy.

gameplay.strongest: It gives players the strongest in-the-moment reason to care: win and the Hand Fill-clicks your decorator so you are coloured in properly, lose and you are 'back to grey, with a sulk'. It is the only variant that honestly squares the hidden total with split-screen players seeing nearby paint ('you can't see a picture from inside it', and the fiction covers the total, not the local view). It fixes the palette arithmetic so every pair can legally win. The Frame / untitled (n) gallery of real final canvases is progression built from actual play. 'Close your lines' ties the Bucket's leak mechanic to the world.
gameplay.weakest: Mute colours give the pair matchup no drama or identity, so random pairs are only 'Hand moods'. Fourteen named greys against four seats implies character selection the box-head art cannot support. The 2v2 rivalry is soft ('mates in the pub').

production.strongest: It has the best production fit and tone consistency. 'The Hand cannot draw hands, so everyone holds a tool' explains the crude art style and why box-heads carry weapons. The colours are mute tins, so there is almost no per-colour dialogue to write or localise. A trade union replaces the churches, which removes the religion risk entirely and lands the author's 'painter tradesmen' hint. Black plus 14 greys plus one free slot fixes the palette arithmetic, so every pair is a clean contest. Winners being filled in only on the players keeps the art rule intact. The Frame (real end-of-match canvas thumbnails named untitled (n)) is cheap because the paint map already exists, and it is honest progression.
production.weakest: 'Grey people longing for colour' leans melancholy and needs constant comic counterweight. Fourteen named greys with dreams implies distinct characters that the identical box-head art cannot show, and the dreams are an open-ended writing cost. 'Save changes to untitled?' wording plus a two-tin left/right button scheme still evokes one specific program, although the variant itself offers a retitle fallback ('Keep this one?'). Mute colours give less drama.

variants.name: Save Changes to untitled?
variants.angle: This version turns the colours from abstract teams into a cast of petty minor gods running for office. Each one is an election candidate with a recognisable personality, and the greys are former candidates who lost. The election framing gives the theology an engine without borrowing from any real faith, and the cast produces new jokes every match instead of repeating one meta gag.
variants.logline: The universe is an unsaved drawing with one palette slot left, and five vain little colour gods are running for it. When the Hand finally clicks Save, the colour covering most of the canvas gets the slot for good, and the loser gets dithered down to grey and joins the fourteen other gods who lost.
variants.world:
Creation is a file called "untitled", open in a crude drawing program called Scrawl. Scrawl is drawn badly on purpose, and its only buttons are the ones the Hand can be bothered to draw. The file has never been saved, so nothing in it is permanent yet. That includes the ground, the sky and you.

Scrawl's palette has 16 slots. Black holds slot 1 and does a job, not a campaign (see below). Slots 2 to 15 are fourteen greys. Every grey is a god who once ran for the last slot and lost: Grey 4 was Purple, Grey 9 was Teal, and Grey 11 was Beige, who mostly lost to apathy. Slot 16 is EMPTY, and the whole world is organised around that emptiness.

That explains the look. The world is grey because greys are all that is left, the dark value under the paint is the oldest loser, and the black keyline is the one god who is never on the ballot. Team hues never appear in the scenery because no colour has been elected yet. A colour on the ground is a campaign promise, not a fact.

The Sun is drawn in grey with a hand-written label: "SUN (COLOUR PENDING)". All five candidates have promised it to their voters.
variants.the_colours:
There are five candidates, all of them small, vain, sure they deserve it, and running in pairs because the ballot only has room for two names.

BLUE, "The Sensible Choice": Blue thinks the vacancy is a clerical error and the slot was always his ("Who do you think the sky was waiting for?"). He is calm and condescending, and his campaign material is memos. He appears in two of the three pairs because he enters every election. His career record is excellent, and he is somehow never in office. Slogan: "BE REASONABLE."

ORANGE, "The Hazard": Loud, high-visibility and populist. He talks entirely in warning signs and is deeply sensitive about the fruit ("THE FRUIT IS NAMED AFTER ME. CHECK THE DATES."). He brings a traffic cone to the debate. Slogan: "CAUTION: WINNING."

PINK, "The Main Character": Theatrical and fashionable, the cast's quiet nod to Splatoon's squid kids. She will not be called "light red". She campaigns with an entrance and treats every loss as a costume change. Slogan: "PINK IS NOT A SHADE. PINK IS A DECISION."

GREEN, "The Grassroots": Earnest and patient, with a forty-year plan and a compost heap. Blue and Yellow both claim Green is just the two of them mixed. Green finds this deeply hurtful and keeps a laminated certificate reading "100% NOT A MIX". Slogan: "THE GRASS REMEMBERS."

YELLOW, "The Sunny Disposition": Relentlessly upbeat and somewhat aggressive about it. Yellow thinks the Sun has already endorsed them, waves at it constantly, and treats it as a running mate. Yellow is the most likely to say "no hard feelings" in a way that suggests very hard feelings. Slogan: "VOTE BRIGHT. OR ELSE :)"

THE GREYS are the fourteen former candidates, now gods of shading. They are not dead. They are retired, unionised, and live in the backdrop, where they heckle. Each kept one habit of their old personality: Grey 4 (ex-Purple) is still regal about being a shadow, and Grey 9 (ex-Teal) insists the last count was rigged. They are the chorus, and they are the game's best supply of jokes.

BLACK, "The Keyline": The only god with a job. Black outlines everything, campaigns for nothing, and says nothing. Black is also the reason the Bucket stops at walls. Every god resents and needs the Keyline.
variants.the_creator:
The Hand, the user of Scrawl, owns the file. The Hand does not know the gods exist. It is not a deity, judge or parent. It is somebody idly doodling who will, at some unknown moment, click Save. It draws badly, hums (in the sense that its cursor wobbles), gets distracted, and once left the file open overnight. It has two buttons, and nobody has worked out what the right one does.

Every candidate claims the Hand's endorsement on no evidence at all. "The Hand moved slightly towards us" is a regular campaign headline. Keeping the Hand oblivious and slightly goofy stops it reading as a stand-in for a real god.
variants.who_you_play:
You play the volunteers: box-head drawings, the only kind of person the Hand can draw. A box, two dots, a line, and a flat stroke on top, which is how the Hand draws hair and which the box-heads call a cap out of politeness. The overalls are the only part of a box-head the Hand ever filled in, so they are the only place a candidate's colour can be worn. Putting on coloured overalls means signing up for a campaign.

Box-heads are not gods, and they don't worship anyone. They are a workforce: canvassers, poster-hangers and paint-throwers who were roped in. Some are true believers, and some are there for the free overalls.
variants.why_they_fight:
The stake for the gods is permanence. The winner is saved into slot 16 and exists in the file for good, and the loser becomes Grey 16½ (the palette is very full).

The stake for the box-heads is more selfish and more urgent. **An unsaved file can be lost.** If the Hand closes Scrawl without saving, everything, box-heads included, goes back to the blank before the file was opened. The Hand will only click Save when the picture looks finished, and a canvas split evenly between two colours does not look finished. A tie means the Hand shrugs and clicks "Don't Save". Both teams of box-heads therefore need SOMEBODY to win clearly. They fight hard for their own colour, but under it they fight for the canvas to look decided.

There is also a personal stake. A box-head whose colour wins keeps coloured overalls for good: they are Saved, and stand a little taller. A box-head whose colour loses gets grey overalls and a background job. That is not fatal, just mildly humiliating. (The greys say the background has excellent benefits.)

The score stays hidden because a picture does not add itself up while it is still being drawn, and because every god runs internal polling that is always wrong. During a match, each god claims a landslide.
variants.reveal_and_rematch:
REVEAL: The match freezes. The Hand's cursor drifts into view. A crude, wobbly dialog is drawn in front of the action one stroke at a time: "Save changes to untitled?" with three hand-lettered buttons, YES / NO / CANCEL. The cursor hovers over NO for one awful beat, then over CANCEL, then clicks YES. A progress bar drawn as a row of scribbled boxes crawls along as the pixels are counted, and the greys in the backdrop lean forward. The bar fills. Slot 16 shows the winner's colour, and the losing colour dithers to grey one row at a time, from the top of the screen down, crossing the losing box-heads' overalls last.

The loser gives a one-line concession speech in its own colour just before it greys out ("I'd like to thank the Grass." / "THIS IS A HAZARD." / "Darling, I'll be back in a better outfit."). The winner gives a victory line that is usually too long, and the Hand cuts it off by starting to draw again.

REMATCH: The win never lasts, because the Hand never stops. Two seconds after saving, it doodles one more stroke, the title bar picks up its little "*", and the file is unsaved again. Scrawl only commits slot 16 on a clean save, so a single new stroke puts the slot back up for grabs. The greys groan. The loser, still half dithered, files an appeal. The rematch button is DEMAND A RECOUNT. Whichever button you pick, the next election starts at once with a freshly drawn pair, so a losing god can be back on the ballot straight away with its colour restored "pending appeal".
variants.pairs_explained:
The ballot only has room for two names, and each authored pair is a long-running feud with a name and a backstory.

BLUE vs ORANGE, "The Old Feud": Opposites on the colour wheel. Each thinks the other exists only to make them look good. Debates are mostly Orange shouting and Blue writing "noted".

PINK vs GREEN, "The Garden Party": One flowerbed, two claims. Pink says flowers are what a garden is for, and Green says the garden is the leaves and the flowers are decoration. Both are partly right, and neither will ever say so. Every arena in this pairing gets a hand-drawn grey flower that both sides insist is theirs.

BLUE vs YELLOW, "The Custody Battle": These two are allegedly Green's parents, and they are running against each other while Green watches from the crowd and refuses to endorse either ("I am NOT a mix."). Blue is in this pairing too because Blue enters every election.

New pairs are new feuds. Any future colour pair arrives with an invented grudge rather than a balance number, so adding a pair to the content list also means writing a backstory.
variants.weapons:
Every weapon is a Scrawl tool, drawn crude and treated by the candidates as sacred campaign equipment.

SPRAYER = the Speckle Can. Scrawl's spray tool, the most-used tool in every campaign. It throws a cloud of dots and covers a lot of ground quickly. Every god claims to have invented it. Orange holds it like a megaphone.

ROLLER = the Fat Brush. The Hand's widest square brush tip, which leaves a solid stripe like a billboard. It is Blue's favourite because it is "thorough".

BUCKET = the Flood. Fill-with-colour. It floods any enclosed shape and stops only at the Keyline. Every gap in a line is a moral failing, and greys draw little warning signs on leaky walls. It is Pink's favourite: one gesture, total coverage, very dramatic.

MISTER = the Rumour. The smallest spray nozzle, which puts down a faint scatter of dots, so a colour is "barely there but everybody heard". It is Green's favourite, because Green believes in slow, patient influence.

Weapon pickup lines change with the god: Yellow hands you a Speckle Can with "this one's a happy can :)", and Orange hands you the same can with "THIS IS NOT A TOY. IT IS A STATEMENT."
arenas: The Margin (Close Quarters): the cramped strip along the edge of the canvas where the Hand never draws anything on purpose. Tight, crowded, all elbows.
The Podium (King of the Hill): a lump drawn with the curve tool, used for the debate. Whoever holds the top is 'the frontrunner' until they fall off.
The Wobble (Turbulence): the Hand has had coffee. Platforms jitter and drift as the cursor shakes, and every god blames this on the other.
Warm-Up Scribbles (Movement Course): the corner where the Hand tests its strokes before drawing anything real. Loops, zig-zags and abandoned spirals. The greys run it as a training camp.
Mid-Undo: someone is holding the undo shortcut, and chunks of the arena blink in and out of existence. No candidate will admit to wanting to undo anything.
The Selection: a rectangle of marching ants being dragged slowly across the canvas, carrying the arena with it. Both campaigns claim the Hand is moving it 'towards us'.
800%: the magnified view, where every pixel is a block you can stand on and one stray dot from the Rumour is a cliff.
The Grey Hall: the backdrop where the fourteen retired gods live. A mausoleum-shaped retirement home drawn in loving greyscale. The greys watch from the balconies.
variants.menus_and_meta:
TITLE: The game opens on a crude, hand-drawn "Save changes to untitled?" dialog. YES starts a match, NO opens options ("Not now, maybe later"), and CANCEL quits with the caption "The Hand closed the program. Nothing was lost, because nothing was saved." The Hand's cursor wobbles around the screen while you choose.

TEAM SELECT = THE BALLOT: A ballot slip is drawn on screen and the random pair is announced as an election, "THIS ELECTION: PINK vs GREEN — THE GARDEN PARTY". Picking a side means pulling on that god's overalls. Each god gets one fixed campaign poster, drawn crude in their colour and slogan. The posters double as loading screens.

DURING PLAY: No score, only "internal polling" captions in each god's colour, which are confidently and comically wrong. A grey heckler line appears now and then.

RESULTS: The save dialog reveal, then a "Palette" strip along the bottom with fifteen slots plus slot 16 showing the current winner, then the concession and victory lines, then DEMAND A RECOUNT (rematch) or LEAVE THE CANVAS (back to menu).

PROGRESSION AND UNLOCKS:
1. Each god keeps a career record: elections run, slot-16 tenures, longest stretch "saved" (always a few seconds).
2. The Grey Hall can be unlocked one portrait at a time: each grey's former colour name and a single line of backstory ("Grey 6, formerly Lavender. Lost to Beige. Still not over it."). The unlocks are lore, not power.
3. Optional cosmetic caps and cap stickers based on campaign merch ("I VOTED BRIGHT").
4. A "Hall of Saves" in the save data that records which god held the slot at the end of each session, as a long-running cross-session joke.
variants.escalation:
The gods are what keeps this from being one joke: five petty personalities in permanent campaign mode produce endless small material.

1. ATTACK ADS AND CAMPAIGN CAPTIONS: Each pairing gets its own lines on loading screens and between rounds. "ORANGE: SEEN STANDING NEAR GREY 3. COINCIDENCE?" "BLUE: HAS NEVER TOUCHED A SUNSET." "GREEN: ALLEGEDLY BLUE AND YELLOW. GREEN DENIES."
2. SCANDALS AS ARENA EVENTS: The arena gimmicks are stories. The Wobble is "the Hand is shaky, and both sides say it's the other's fault", and Mid-Undo is "someone is trying to undo the vote".
3. THE GREYS AS A GROWING CAST: Every grey is a ready-made character, and new heckling lines and Grey Hall portraits can be added indefinitely. A god who loses a lot "earns" a grey number as a running gag ("Blue: provisionally assigned Grey 17 'just in case'").
4. CROSS-PAIR GOSSIP: Gods who sit out an election still comment. Green won't stop endorsing nobody in the Custody Battle, and Pink critiques everyone's outfit.
5. SESSION MEMORY: The career records feed the lines ("ORANGE has lost three elections tonight. ORANGE would like a fourth.").
6. CONTENT GROWTH: Any new colour pair is a new candidate with a new feud. Any new weapon is a new Scrawl tool that gods fight over, any new arena is somewhere new on the canvas or a new Hand mood, and any new mode is a new election rule (a runoff, a recount, "the Hand is drawing a second picture").
7. THE LONG GAG: The Sun. It stays grey the whole game, labelled COLOUR PENDING. Every god has promised it to their voters. It never gets a colour, and the joke gets better the longer it stays grey.
