variants.name_options:
PROGRAM: "Scrawl" (invented, generic, crude). Alternatives are "Daub" and "Smudge". It should never be called Paint, nor anything ending in ".exe", and it should not use any real program's icon or dialog layout. Every window is drawn freehand in the art style.

FILE: "untitled", a generic placeholder that every program uses, so it carries no brand. The world is "the Canvas", and in-world it is simply "the Picture".

PEOPLE: "box-heads" (casual) or "volunteers" (in the campaign framing). GODS: "the Candidates", and collectively "the Palette". FORMER GODS: "the Greys", "the Retired", or "the Shading".

GAME TITLE: "Colour Wars" still fits, arguably better than before, since it is now a literal war between colours who are characters. Recommendation: keep COLOUR WARS as the title and use "Save changes to untitled?" as the tagline and the title-screen dialog ("COLOUR WARS — Save changes to untitled?"). The repository name, the executable and every identifier stay as they are.
variants.risks:
1. RELIGION REGISTER: "Gods", "theology" and "commandments" can drift into parodying real faiths. Mitigations: write the gods as politicians on a campaign, not as objects of worship. No prayer, scripture verses, prophets, sacrifices, temples or "thou shalt"-style language, and box-heads are volunteers, not worshippers. The judges' line THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL has been deliberately rewritten as "RULE ONE OF THE CANVAS". Keep the Hand an oblivious doodler, never a creator-deity who judges anyone.

2. EXPRESSING THE GODS VISUALLY: The art direction says team hues appear only in paint and on players, so the gods have no bodies. Their personality has to come through captions in their colour, posters (menus only), paint patterns and concession lines. That is a lot of text for a couch game where people skip text. Mitigation: lines are one sentence, and a god's personality must work from slogan + poster + one concession line alone.

3. ONE-JOKE META: The palette joke still carries everything. The cast helps, but if the gods feel interchangeable it collapses back into a single gag. Each god needs a distinct verbal tic that holds up in five words.

4. BLUE IS OVER-REPRESENTED: Blue appears in two of the three pairs. That is written into the joke ("Blue enters every election"), but players may notice Blue more often and that has to read as intended.

5. GRIMNESS: Being dithered to grey could read as death or erasure. Keep it firmly as retirement, demotion and a job in shading, with greys who are cheerful, unionised and heckling. The "unsaved file can be lost" stake must stay abstract and comic, never shown.

6. PERIOD-PIECE AND IMPERSONATION: A 16-colour drawing program with a save dialog reads as late-90s software no matter what. Mitigations: no dates (the old "since 1998" is dropped), no real UI layouts, icons, fonts or program names. YES/NO/CANCEL and "untitled" are generic, but the dialog must always be drawn freehand and must never look like a recreation of any real operating system's dialog.

7. COLOURBLINDNESS: Pink/green is a hard pair. Making the gods characters with names and slogans helps a little, but paint readability still needs its own solution (patterns or value contrast), and the premise does not fix that.

8. SCOPE CREEP: The Grey Hall, career records and captions are cheap to write but add up to a content commitment. They should be layered on after the core loop and reveal ship, not before.

longevity.strongest: The fourteen greys are former candidates who lost. That one move explains the grey world from inside the fiction, turns the art constraint into lore, and gives an endless chorus of characters (Grey 9, formerly Teal, demanding a recount). The pitch works in one breath: 'five vain colours are running for the last palette slot, and the losers become the greys.' Long gags like SUN (COLOUR PENDING), the tie meaning 'Don't Save', and the '*' re-dirtying the file for the rematch all keep the slot fight at the centre.
longevity.weakest: The gods have no bodies under the art rules, so their personalities can only reach players through text and posters, which couch players skip. The word 'gods' still carries a little religion risk even after the rewrite into politicians. Blue appearing in two pairs strains the idea of a single consistent character.

gameplay.strongest: It has the best explanation of the grey world: the greys are former losing candidates, black is the one god never on the ballot, and 'a colour on the ground is a campaign promise, not a fact'. Pair feuds give each random draw an identity. The rematch is in-fiction: one more stroke, the '*' returns, the file is unsaved again, and DEMAND A RECOUNT. The winners keep coloured overalls and the losers get grey overalls and a background job. That personal stake shows on the player models themselves.
gameplay.weakest: The tie stake ('a tie means Don't Save, so both sides need someone to win clearly') is a confusing motive that does nothing in play. The 'internal polling' captions shown during play risk being read as score hints. It barely addresses split screen or respawn. The gods have no bodies, so their personality depends on text.

production.strongest: Greys as former candidates who lost (Grey 9, ex-Teal) explains the grey world, the dark value and the keyline in a single move. Black as the Keyline that 'campaigns for nothing' and stops the Bucket is a neat rule. The concession lines are cheap and the right length. 'THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL' is rewritten as 'RULE ONE OF THE CANVAS'.
production.weakest: It still calls the colours 'gods' and puts the retired greys in a mausoleum-shaped hall, so religion and death readings stay live while denying them. 'If the Hand closes without saving, everything returns to blank' and a tie meaning Don't Save add an existential stake with no game mechanic behind it. It carries the heaviest text load (five personalities, greys' heckling, attack ads, career records) for a couch game where players skip text. 'Scrawl' needs a real-app collision check.

variants.name: Save Changes to untitled? (The Election Version)
variants.angle: This version takes out the gods and the churches. The last palette slot is now an election. The colours are candidates who become characters through their campaigns. The box-heads are canvassers and voters who need polling day to happen. A painted pixel is a ballot and the Save is polling day. The fixed core is unchanged and is now told through civic process (manifestos, a returning officer, recounts, by-elections) rather than scripture. This keeps it away from real religion and gives it a format that keeps producing new jokes.
variants.logline: The whole world is an unsaved drawing with one palette slot left, and two colours are standing for it. Your box-head canvassers paint every surface in their candidate's colour, because when the Hand finally clicks Save, every pixel counts as a vote and the loser goes back to grey.
variants.world: The world is a single picture called untitled, open in a crude drawing program that is never named on screen. It is drawn in the author's own hand and calls itself DAUB at most. The palette holds sixteen colours. Black, white and thirteen greys came with it, which is why the world is grey with a dark value underneath and a black keyline around everything. Slot 16 has been empty for as long as the clock has said 12:00 AM, which is always. Nothing has ever been saved, so nothing here has ever been permanent, and nobody minds much because nobody remembers otherwise. The program has one law: a colour that is not in the palette cannot be saved. So when someone mixes a new colour in the Edit Colours box, slot 16 is up for election. The rules are posted on a grey noticeboard in every arena. (1) Each pixel is one ballot. (2) A pixel painted twice counts for the latest coat; there are no spoilt ballots, only overruled ones. (3) Polling day is whenever the Hand clicks Save. (4) Counting the votes before the save is illegal, because a picture does not add itself up while it is still being drawn. Rule 4 is why the score is hidden. Exit polls are banned by law, and a crude exit pollster with a clipboard appears in the backdrop looking guilty. Campaigning has covered the world. Every arena has grey billboards and fly-posters with slogans in the author's handwriting. The posters are grey too, because a candidate's colour may only appear on ballots (paint) and on their own canvassers. Electoral law forbids putting it anywhere else.
variants.the_colours:
Every colour is a candidate standing for slot 16. Each has a manifesto, a slogan, and a personality that comes through what it posts and promises. None of them maps onto real politics. Each one campaigns on what it is as a colour.

BLUE is the perennial candidate. It has stood in every election since the clock began, which is why it is on two ballots. It has won many times and been forgotten every time the program closed. Blue is calm, a little tired, and always technically correct. Slogan: "BLUE. YOU KNOW WHERE YOU ARE WITH BLUE." Manifesto points: skies, water, 'the default for a hyperlink'. Its attack ads are mild: "ORANGE HAS NEVER BEEN A SKY."

ORANGE is the loud populist of traffic cones and safety vests. Its posters are mostly exclamation marks, and its whole platform is visibility. Slogan: "YOU CAN'T IGNORE ORANGE (LEGALLY, ON A ROAD)." It claims to be a mix of two primary colours, so it represents more people. Attack ad: "BLUE IS JUST GREY THAT WENT TO UNIVERSITY."

PINK is the celebrity outsider who has never held a slot and says so with pride. It is all charisma, glitter and no policy. Slogan: "PINK: IT'S ABOUT TIME." Manifesto: "Fun. More of it." Attack ad: "GREEN IS THE COLOUR OF MOULD."

GREEN is the grassroots candidate. It is earnest, does door-to-door, and has a three-page manifesto that nobody reads. Slogan: "GREEN: GROWING ON YOU." (Pun on grass only. It does not stand for any real party.) It is very proud of the endorsement 'most leaves'. Attack ad: "PINK HAS NO POLICIES. WE CHECKED. THE PAGE WAS BLANK. (IT WAS ALSO PINK.)"

YELLOW is the cheerful optimist who keeps being mistaken for the Sun and has to file a correction every election. Slogan: "YELLOW: NOT THE SUN. BUT SIMILAR!" It promises bananas, highlighters and 'the good kind of caution'. Attack ad on Blue, delivered warmly: "BLUE HAS HAD ITS TURN. MANY TURNS. HAS ANYONE SEEN BLUE'S TURNS? THEY WERE NOT SAVED."

Candidates never appear as figures. They are present only through their colour, their posters and their voice in the captions, so the world keeps its rule of no team hues outside paint and players.
variants.the_creator:
THE HAND is a crude cursor hand floating above the canvas. It is not a god and it does not vote. Its only power is calling polling day. It holds no views and is not even watching most of the time. It drifts, hovers, occasionally draws a wobbly line through the backdrop and wanders off. The colours court it anyway, with posters in the backdrop that face upward ("HAND: PLEASE SAVE"). It appears clearly in only three moments: just before the match ends it hovers toward the top of the screen, it clicks Save at the reveal, and it clicks Close for a rematch.

THE RETURNING OFFICER is the progress bar. It is the only official in the world: a long grey rectangle with a face, the same two dots and a line as the box-heads, lying on its side. It is very slow, very proper and completely neutral. It speaks in formal declarations and tallies every pixel during the reveal. It is the closest thing the game has to a mascot and the voice of the menus.
variants.who_you_play: You play a box-head canvasser: a drawing the Hand made, because that is the only person it knows how to draw. A square head, two dots, a line, a flat cap (the Hand's one stroke for hair) and overalls. The overalls are the only part the Hand ever filled in, so they are the one place a canvasser can wear their candidate's colour. In effect they are a rosette you live inside. Box-heads are decorators by trade. Campaigns hire them because they are the only people in the picture who own rollers, so every match is a canvassing shift: you paint the town and knock the other side's canvassers back to campaign HQ (respawn). Teams of two are a campaign ward, and four players are two rival canvassing teams on the same street.
variants.why_they_fight: The box-heads have personal stakes, not just a candidate's. (1) THEY HAVE NEVER BEEN SAVED EITHER. An unsaved drawing exists only until the program closes, so polling day is the one moment anyone in the picture becomes permanent. Box-heads want an election because they want a save; the colour is almost secondary. (2) THE WINNING SIDE IS SAVED IN COLOUR. When the file saves, the winning canvassers' overalls are written to disk in the new colour. The losers are saved too, but their overalls dither to the nearest grey. Losing never erases you. You are saved as nobody in particular, which is a quiet and very funny fate rather than a grim one. (3) WORK. Canvassers are paid per square metre of ballot. Nobody has ever seen this pay, because wages are also unsaved. (4) IT IS A TOWN THEY LIVE IN. Whatever colour wins becomes the only colour the next drawing can be made in, so the box-heads are choosing the look of their own future.
variants.reveal_and_rematch:
REVEAL (polling day): the match clock hits zero and everything freezes mid-splat. The Hand drifts in. A crude box drawn in the author's own wobbly style, not a real dialog layout, appears with the words "Save changes to untitled?" and three hand-drawn buttons: YES / NO / UH. The Hand clicks YES. The Returning Officer progress bar slides in and reads in caption text: "I, THE PROGRESS BAR, BEING THE RETURNING OFFICER FOR THE CONSTITUENCY OF UNTITLED, DO HEREBY BEGIN COUNTING." It fills slowly while the existing paint-tally reveal runs. At the end it declares: "BLUE: 51.3% OF THE PICTURE. I DECLARE BLUE DULY ELECTED TO SLOT 16." The losing colour dithers row by row into grey checkerboard, and the losing canvassers' overalls grey out with it. The winners' colour appears in slot 16 of a palette strip, which for the first time in the match shows a team hue outside paint and players.

RECOUNT: if the margin is under a small threshold (for example 1%), the Returning Officer says "THE MARGIN IS NARROW. A RECOUNT HAS BEEN REQUESTED. (BY ME. I AM NERVOUS.)" The bar empties and refills once, faster, before the same declaration. This is pure theatre that stretches tension on close games without changing the result.

REMATCH (by-election): the Hand closes the program. A hand-drawn "untitled was saved." appears, then the screen goes black, then the program opens again. The palette has forgotten everything and slot 16 is empty: "A BY-ELECTION HAS BEEN CALLED. (THE PROGRAM WAS CLOSED.)" This explains why no win lasts and why the next match always starts in grey. Declining the rematch returns to the menu with the Hand's "NO" leaving a little sadness behind.
variants.pairs_explained: The Edit Colours box is the ballot paper and it only has room for two names, so every election is a two-candidate race. The authored pairs are the registered contests: BLUE vs ORANGE ('The Classic', the safe seat that never stays safe), PINK vs GREEN ('The Garden Party', glamour against grassroots), BLUE vs YELLOW ('Sky vs Sun', which Yellow insists is not what it is about). Blue being on two ballots is a running joke rather than a balance quirk: Blue is the perennial candidate and is on the ballot whether anyone asked or not. The random draw at match start is the nominations closing, shown as "NOMINATIONS HAVE CLOSED. TWO CANDIDATES ARE STANDING." Future pairs arrive as newly registered candidates, each with its own manifesto, which is the main content pipeline.
variants.weapons:
The weapons are campaign materials, and box-heads use their own decorating tools.
SPRAYER = THE LEAFLET DROP: an airbrush that scatters ballots far and wide, for door-to-door coverage. Item text: "Reaches every letterbox. Also every wall."
ROLLER = THE FLY-POSTER: a wide decorator's roller for pasting your candidate over everything in a straight line. Item text: "One poster. Very long."
BUCKET = THE LANDSLIDE: Fill With Colour in a bucket. It floods an area and leaks through any gap in a line, which is a joke about loose border lines. Item text: "Floods safe seats. Check your boundaries."
MISTER = THE WHISPER CAMPAIGN: the smallest airbrush nozzle. It leaves a faint drift of colour that adds up. Item text: "A rumour of colour. Rumours count."
Splatting an opponent = "CANVASSER SENT BACK TO HQ". The respawn point is campaign HQ, a grey portakabin with a flat-capped box-head drinking tea. Overlapping paint is never a spoilt ballot; the later coat simply overrules it, which matches the actual paint rules.
arenas: CLOSE QUARTERS = THE MARGINAL: a tight terrace street where three doors decide everything. Posters: 'EVERY PIXEL COUNTS (THERE ARE ONLY 40 HERE)'.
KING OF THE HILL = THE SOAPBOX: one raised crate in the town square; whoever holds it is 'addressing the electorate'. The Hand sometimes hovers over it like a camera crew.

TURBULENCE = THE SWING SEAT: a windy constituency where paint drifts and votes drift with it. Weathervane posters point at whichever team is leading, which is illegal under Rule 4, so they spin wildly to stay deniable.
MOVEMENT COURSE = THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL: a solo route of rooftops, billboards and a battle bus drawn as a rectangle with two circles. Route times are 'stump speeches'.
THE MARGIN: the white strip at the edge of the canvas where the Hand never draws; platforms are half-finished lines and a sign reads 'UNREPRESENTED'.
THE COUNT HALL: grey trestle tables, ballot boxes that are just squares, and the Returning Officer lying asleep along one wall. Painting it near the end of a match is considered rude.

BOUNDARY REVIEW: an arena whose dividing walls are being redrawn mid-match by the Hand's wobbly line tool, so a gap can open and let a Landslide through. Gerrymandering as level design, with no real-world referent.
variants.menus_and_meta: TITLE: the program opens on a blank grey canvas with the Hand hovering. The title is drawn in the author's crude lettering, with a palette strip below whose last slot blinks empty ("SLOT 16: VACANT"). Press Start = "OPEN untitled". TEAM SELECT = NOMINATIONS: two hand-drawn ballot columns with candidate names and slogans. Players walk their box-head under a column to join that campaign, and their overalls fill with the candidate's colour as they sign. Stage select = "CHOOSE A CONSTITUENCY". Settings = "THE ELECTORAL COMMISSION", which runs to a single grey room with the Returning Officer behind a desk. Match length is "CAMPAIGN LENGTH". RESULTS = THE DECLARATION: the per-player breakdown is printed as the Returning Officer's official returns ("BALLOTS CAST BY CANVASSER 2: 1,204 PIXELS"), with categories like "Most Doors Knocked" (most paint), "Most Rivals Sent to HQ" and "Quietest Campaign" (the mister). PROGRESSION = THE PALETTE HISTORY: a strip of every slot-16 winner from past matches, labelled "THE BRIEFLY ELECTED", one swatch per match. It is the only thing the program remembers, and it does so against its own rules; the Returning Officer will not discuss how. UNLOCKS = NEWLY REGISTERED CANDIDATES (new colour pairs, each with a manifesto card and three slogans), new campaign posters that redecorate the arenas, and cap variants that are still one flat stroke but tilted. PAUSE = "THE HAND HAS GONE TO MAKE A CUP OF TEA", with the Hand absent from the canvas.
variants.escalation: The premise generates content rather than repeating one gag. (1) EVERY CANDIDATE IS A WRITING PROMPT. A new pair needs a manifesto, slogans, two attack ads each way and a declaration line, which suits a small team and the crude art style. (2) ELECTION VOCABULARY IS DEEP: hustings, swing, turnout, safe seats, boundary review, postal votes (a weapon-pickup idea), a hung canvas (an exact tie, which is very rare and gets a special 'HUNG CANVAS - THE HAND WILL HAVE TO DECIDE' screen where the Hand flips a coin), and snap elections (a shortened match variant called when the Hand 'gets bored'). (3) THE BACKDROP CHANGES BETWEEN MATCHES. Posters and billboards can respond to the last result: the winner's posters get smug ("THANK YOU, UNTITLED"), the loser's get bitter, then everything is torn down at the by-election. Shared memory of the Palette History lets posters refer to streaks ("BLUE: 4 TERMS. NONE REMEMBERED."). (4) CROSS-CANDIDATE FEUDS: Blue against everyone, Yellow's ongoing legal distinction from the Sun, Pink and Green's feud over who owns flowers. These can be teased through new arena posters. (5) EVENTS: a 'Leaders' Debate' night with mirrored arenas, a 'Coalition' 2v2 variant where team colours blend in the reveal and the Returning Officer refuses to allow it ('THERE IS ONE SLOT'), and an 'Independent' novelty run in which grey stands as a candidate and nobody can tell if it is winning.
tone_captions: SLOT 16: VACANT. NOMINATIONS ARE OPEN.
RULE 4: NO COUNTING UNTIL THE SAVE. A PICTURE DOES NOT ADD ITSELF UP WHILE IT IS STILL BEING DRAWN.
CANVASSER SENT BACK TO HQ. THE KETTLE IS ON.
EXIT POLLS ARE ILLEGAL. PLEASE STOP ASKING THE WEATHERVANE.
YELLOW WISHES TO CLARIFY THAT IT IS NOT, AND HAS NEVER BEEN, THE SUN.
I, THE PROGRESS BAR, DECLARE ORANGE DULY ELECTED TO SLOT 16. PLEASE REMAIN CALM. I AM 40% CALM.
THE MARGIN IS NARROW. A RECOUNT HAS BEEN REQUESTED. (BY ME.)
THE LOSING CANDIDATE HAS BEEN DITHERED TO THE NEAREST GREY. IT IS TAKING IT WELL.
A BY-ELECTION HAS BEEN CALLED. (THE PROGRAM WAS CLOSED.)
BLUE: STANDING SINCE 12:00 AM. ELECTED MANY TIMES. REMEMBERED ZERO.
variants.name_options: PROGRAM: never named on screen if possible; at most a crude invented name. Candidates: DAUB (preferred: short, a painter's word, looks nothing like a real product), SCRIBBLER, or PAINT16 (riskier, too close to the real thing). No logo; the program is only ever a grey frame drawn by hand. FILE: 'untitled' in lower case and nothing more. Avoid '.bmp' and 640x480 on screen, since those date and point it. WORLD/PLACE: 'the Constituency of untitled', or 'the Canvas' in short. OFFICIAL: 'the Returning Officer'. ACTS: 'polling day' (the save) and 'a by-election' (the rematch). GAME TITLE: 'Colour Wars' still fits and is the better shelf title. The joke is that it is not really a war but an election held by other means, and the plain title lets the premise surprise. A strapline can carry the joke: 'COLOUR WARS - Save changes to untitled?' or 'COLOUR WARS: THE ELECTION FOR SLOT 16'. 'Save Changes to untitled?' works better as the name of the reveal moment than as the box title.
variants.risks: 1) REAL POLITICS CREEP. Civic satire attracts readings: Green as a real party, Blue and Orange (and others) as real parties in some countries, 'populist' coding, attack-ad tone. Mitigations: every candidate campaigns only on what it is as a colour, never on policy, ideology, nations or people; no left or right coding; never mimic real campaign branding. Some players will read real parties into colours anyway, especially Blue, Orange and Green, so an author pass per region is worth it. 2) UK-SPECIFIC VOCABULARY. 'Returning officer', 'by-election', 'hustings', and 'fly-poster' are British/Commonwealth terms and may not land elsewhere. The jokes still work as plain deadpan officialese, but a US player may miss 'duly elected'. 3) STILL ONE META JOKE UNDERNEATH. 'It is secretly a paint program' is now a frame rather than the punchline, but heavy captions could tire. Keep the text short and rare; the reveal and the posters should do most of the work. 4) TEXT-HEAVY HUMOUR IN A SPLIT-SCREEN ACTION GAME. Players will not read posters mid-fight. Comedy has to live in the reveal, menus, backdrop art and short splat or respawn lines, and fail gracefully if unread. 5) SOFTWARE IMITATION. The 'Save changes?' box and a cursor hand are generic, but a grey frame plus a 16-swatch strip plus a progress bar is close to a specific nostalgic program. Every piece must be drawn crudely in the author's own style, with no real dialog layout, icons, fonts or names. The YES/NO/UH buttons and the face on the progress bar help push it clearly into parody-by-feel. 6) PERIOD PIECE. 'Unsaved since 12:00 AM' is the only time marker; avoid years, resolutions and file extensions on screen. 7) BLUE IN TWO PAIRS. The joke covers it, but if pairs expand, the perennial-candidate gag only works for one colour. 8) VIOLENCE AT THE POLLS. Shooting canvassers at an election can read as dark if worded badly. Keep it as paint and 'sent back to HQ for tea', never intimidation or suppression language. 9) THE HYBRID PROPOSAL. This version deliberately drops the petty-gods idea. 'THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL' could survive as a rule on the noticeboard ('ELECTORAL LAW 0: THE HAND MAY NOT DRAW WELL'), but bringing deities back reintroduces the religion-satire risk this version was built to avoid. 10) LOSING TO GREY. Losers being 'saved as nobody in particular' must stay funny; the dither animation and the Returning Officer's fussy tone have to carry it so it never reads as erasure.

longevity.strongest: Pixel = ballot and Save = polling day map exactly onto the mechanics. The Returning Officer, a progress bar with a box-head face lying on its side, is a real mascot with a strong comic voice ('I AM 40% CALM'). Election vocabulary gives almost unlimited modes and events: recount theatre on close margins, by-election rematches, a hung canvas, boundary review used as level design, snap elections.
longevity.weakest: Civic satire is the least weird register of the five and pulls toward real party politics (Blue, Orange and Green). The British vocabulary will not travel well. Without gods or retired greys it has no answer for why the world is grey beyond 'the palette came that way', so its lore engine is mostly campaign jokes.

gameplay.strongest: It maps onto the game's systems more completely than any other variant. Rule 4 makes the hidden score a law ('no counting until the Save', exit polls illegal). 'Later coat overrules, no spoilt ballots' matches the actual paint-overwrite rule. Splat = 'sent back to HQ' explains respawn. A team of two is a canvassing ward. All four existing modes get a direct mapping (Marginal, Soapbox, Swing Seat, Campaign Trail). The by-election, where the program closes and the palette forgets, explains why every match starts grey. A recount on narrow margins adds reveal tension without changing the result. Electoral law explains why posters stay grey.
gameplay.weakest: The comedy is text-heavy in a split-screen action game. The UK civic vocabulary and real-party colour readings are risks. The in-match personal stake (being saved in grey, unpaid wages) is spread across four reasons and is weaker than a single sharp want.

production.strongest: The Returning Officer, a progress bar with a box-head face lying on its side, is the cheapest and best mascot in the set: one rectangle, which also gives the reveal its voice. A close-margin recount that empties and refills the bar adds tension at near-zero cost without changing the result. Grey posters with slogans keep hues out of the world. 'Exit polls are illegal' is a clean explanation of the hidden score.
production.weakest: Swapping religion for elections swaps one real-world satire risk for another. Blue, Orange and Green map onto real parties in many countries, and the variant includes 'populist' coding, attack ads, gerrymandering and 'violence at the polls', all of which it flags itself. The vocabulary is UK-specific. It floats PAINT16 as a name option. The scope is broad (Leaders' Debate, Coalition, Independent events).

variants.name: Save Changes to untitled?
variants.angle: Removes the Win98/Paint dependency. The file is now an unsaved drawing in an unnamed, crude, invented drawing program on a device nobody ever sees. The Hand drew a grey world, got bored of colouring it in, and drew little decorators to finish the job. The fight for slot 16 of the palette, and the Save reveal, are unchanged.
variants.logline: Someone drew a grey world, got bored of colouring it in, drew some little decorators in overalls to finish the job, and was called away for tea. The palette has sixteen slots and fifteen are taken by greys and a black. When the Hand comes back and saves, whichever colour covers more of the picture gets the last slot.
variants.world: Creation is a single unsaved picture called untitled. Nobody knows what program it is open in. The program has no name on screen, only the word 'untitled' in a wobbly title strip. Its icons are drawn in the same crude hand as everything else, so they could belong to any drawing program from any decade. The palette is a strip of sixteen square slots along the bottom of the sky. Fourteen are greys, one is black (the keyline everything is outlined in), and slot 16 is an empty dashed square. That covers all of the art direction: the world is grey because nobody has coloured it in yet, the dark value is the shading the Hand did before it lost interest, and the black outline is the only line it ever uses. The Hand is huge, never fully seen, and keeps almost finishing. Its shadow passes over the arenas. When the screen dims for a moment, the box-heads call it night (the device going to sleep). The world's one big landmark is the Sun, a circle with eight lines around it, still uncoloured, and every candidate colour claims it. The background is full of faint grey doodles: a cat with too many legs, a house, a practice signature. They are earlier drafts that never got coloured, and they watch every match like retirees at a bowls club.
variants.the_colours: The colours are candidates, not gods. They are swatches that floated in from the colour picker, each campaigning for slot 16, and they only exist on the canvas while someone paints them. BLUE is the perennial finalist. It turns up in two of the three pairs, has got close to the slot many times and never kept it, and talks as if it is the incumbent. ORANGE says it is 'the Sun's understudy' and says it loudly. YELLOW says the Sun is obviously yellow, that there is no understudy, and that it is being very patient. PINK is all highlighter: it wants to be underlined and thinks being subtle is losing. GREEN is earnest and sure the slot is owed to it 'because of grass', although nobody has drawn any grass. The greys are not candidates. They already have their slots and fill the role of a bored civil service. Grey 9 wants everyone to know it is basically silver.
variants.the_creator: The Hand, plus the unseen someone it belongs to. It drew the world, shaded it, outlined it, and then did what everyone does with colouring-in: drew some little people to do it instead and wandered off. It is not malicious or godlike, just distractible. It is always about to save and always gets called for tea. It never speaks. It is present as a shadow, as the tip of a crude cursor at the edge of the frame, and as its two acts, Save and Undo. The only thing the box-heads know about it for sure is that it can only draw one kind of person.
variants.who_you_play: The decorators. The Hand drew every person the same way: a square head, two dots, a line, and a flat stroke on top that is how it draws hair, which the decorators wear as a cap. It dressed them in overalls because it drew them for a job, and that job is colouring in. They are tradesmen in the literal sense: crews contracted by a colour, with a foreman, a tea break they never get, and strong opinions about rollers. Their overalls are the only part of them the Hand ever filled in, so the overalls are the only place on a person where a candidate colour is allowed to be. They are a crew's uniform, not a flag.
variants.why_they_fight: The candidates fight to exist. The decorators fight to be in the picture that gets kept. After a save, the winning colour is in the palette and everything painted in it stays. The winning crew stays in colour too, so when the picture goes up on the Fridge (the box-heads' word for wherever saved pictures go) they are the ones you can see. The losing crew is not deleted. Their overalls round to the nearest grey and they become background, like the old doodles. Nobody wants that, because background people never get picked for the next job. The decorators are also proud of the work itself: a clean wall, a full fill, nothing missed. There is a trade-pride subplot: the Fill crews and the Brush crews hate each other's work.
variants.reveal_and_rematch: The score is hidden because a picture does not add itself up while it is still being drawn, and nobody counts pixels until someone saves. At the final whistle the match freezes, the Hand's shadow comes over the arena, and a wobbly hand-drawn box appears: 'Save changes to untitled?' The buttons are drawn crudely and are not any real dialog's layout: a big YES, a small no, and a third button scribbled out. The cursor hovers too long, then taps YES. A hand-drawn bar crawls across the screen, 'Counting pixels... (do not move)', and both crews hold a pose. Slot 16 flickers between the two candidates and then fills. A horizontal sweep goes down the canvas like a scanner line, and every pixel of the losing colour rounds to its nearest grey, row by row, along with the losing crew's overalls. The loser plays a small resigned sound rather than a scream. For the rematch, the screen dims (the device sleeps), comes back, and slot 16 is a dashed empty square again with a tiny caption: 'Custom colours are not remembered.' The canvas is still there but the colour is not, so the election runs again every time the program is opened.
variants.pairs_explained: The colour picker never offers a free choice. It offers two suggested swatches, 'Try these!', and the canvas only has room for one more. Each match is one of those suggestions: blue/orange, pink/green or blue/yellow. Blue is in two suggestions because it is the picker's favourite, which is a running gag: Blue has been a finalist more often than anyone and owns slot 16 for exactly one match at a time. Neither colour of a pair is ever in the world itself. A candidate only exists where a decorator has put it, so the rule that team hues appear only in paint and on players is now the plot, not just an art rule.
variants.weapons: These are tools from the program's toolbar, each drawn by the author as a crude icon. None copies a real program's tool set or icons. SPRAYER = 'Fizz', the spray-can tool. The decorators treat it as their best instrument and keep its nozzle clean with a rag. ROLLER = 'Fat Brush', the brush on its biggest square setting, carried like a broom. BUCKET = 'Pour', the fill tool, which leaks through any gap in a line. Close your lines is the first rule of the trade. MISTER = 'Puff', the spray can on its softest setting. Brush crews call it 'a rumour of colour'. Later tools follow the same pattern: Smudge, Stamp, and an Eraser that does not delete but rounds paint back to grey.
arenas: The Sun (King of the Hill): the uncoloured circle at the top of the sky. Whoever is standing on it is colouring the Sun, and both candidates take that very personally.
The Margin (Close Quarters): the cramped strip at the edge of the page where the Hand tests how its pens work. Scribbles, half a star, and a signature practised six times.
Shake to Undo (Turbulence): someone is carrying the device. The canvas lurches, and now and then a platform blinks out of existence and back because the Hand's thumb slipped on Undo.
Warm-Up Scribbles (Movement Course): loops, zigzags and a spiral the Hand drew to get its eye in. They are not very good and they are perfect for running on.
The Old Doodles: an arena built from the abandoned drafts, the many-legged cat, the house with a door too high to reach. The drafts watch from the background.
Zoomed In: the same picture at enormous magnification. Every pixel is a floor tile and every staircase-step line is a staircase.
variants.menus_and_meta: Title screen: the program 'opening'. A crude splash, then 'untitled' fading up, with the empty slot 16 blinking. Team select: the colour picker's 'Try these!' card showing the two suggested swatches, with decorators queuing under each like a hiring hall. Stage select: thumbnails of parts of the same picture, as if the Hand had scrolled around it. HUD: the 16-slot palette strip, fifteen greys and black plus a dashed slot 16 that never shows who is ahead. It only shivers with both colours, which keeps the Splatoon-style hidden score honest. Pause: the Hand looks away and its shadow lifts. Results: the Save box and the counting bar. Progression: the Fridge, a gallery of every saved match as a tiny thumbnail with its winning colour, which slowly turns into a record of the election. Unlocks are new toolbar tools and new suggested pairs. Cosmetics are things the Hand would draw: a pencil behind the ear, a second stroke of hair, a crooked badge. The settings screen could be called 'Brush Size'.
variants.escalation: The premise keeps producing jokes because the Hand keeps adding to the picture and the candidates keep campaigning. New arenas are parts of the drawing the Hand doodled since the last session, and the drafts gossip about them. New pairs arrive from the picker with campaign slogans (Green: 'Grass. Eventually.'). The Sun dispute escalates across updates. The greys get small bureaucratic subplots: Grey 9 petitions to be called silver, and Grey 4 and Grey 5 do not believe they are different. Events come from the device instead of a calendar: Low Battery (the match clock is a battery icon), Rotate (the picture turns sideways for a mode), a Hand doodle that appears mid-match as a new obstacle, and Undo storms. The Fridge history becomes lore: 'Blue held slot 16 for one match in the year of the many-legged cat.' The decorators' trade rivalries grow: Fill crews against Brush crews, apprentices who cannot close a line, a foreman who has not had his tea break since the world was drawn. None of it needs a specific era, brand or piece of hardware.
tone_captions: SLOT 16: EMPTY. PLEASE STOP ASKING.
THE SUN IS GREY UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE.
Pour leaks. Close your lines.
The Hand has been called for tea. Paint quietly.
Counting pixels... (do not move)
Rounding to nearest grey. It doesn't hurt. You just look like everyone else now.
ORANGE: 'I am the Sun's understudy.'  YELLOW: 'There is no understudy.'
Grey 9 would like it noted that it is basically silver.
Custom colours are not remembered.
LOW BATTERY. THE WORLD ENDS AT 3%. (IT DID NOT.)
variants.name_options: The file is 'untitled', with no extension and no format named. It is the only word in the title strip. The program should have no on-screen name. If one is needed in docs, use something generic and invented such as 'the Program' or 'Sketchbox', or call it by its icon, 'the crayon-box app'. Check any working name for real-app collisions, because doodle/sketch app names are crowded. The box-heads call the world 'the Picture', the palette 'the Strip', the empty slot 'Sixteen', and the gallery of saved pictures 'the Fridge'. The crews are 'decorators'. 'Colour Wars' still fits, and fits better than before: it is literally a war between colours over one slot, the decorators are the soldiers, and it is the name the author took back. 'Save Changes to untitled?' works best as the in-world name of the reveal and as a tagline ('Colour Wars: Save changes to untitled?') rather than as the title, because a question as a title is hard to say out loud and to search for.
variants.risks: 1) It could still be one joke. The premise only lasts if the decorators, the candidates and the Hand's distractions produce the ongoing material. If every caption is a software joke it will wear thin, so the trade-crew and Sun-dispute material should carry at least half of it. 2) 'Save changes?', a counting bar and 'custom colours not remembered' are generic, but some players will still read them as nostalgia for one particular old program. Mitigation: never draw a real dialog layout, title bar, toolbar or icon set; keep everything in the author's crude hand; never show a desktop, a taskbar or an OS. 3) A sixteen-colour limit is itself a retro technical idea. The fiction should say 'the Strip has sixteen slots' and never talk about bit depth. 4) Making the Hand someone who gets called for tea leans cosy and childlike. It could undercut the competitive hype or read as a children's game, so the trailer and results moments need some swagger. 5) The hidden score has to stay hidden. The slot-16 HUD element must never give away the lead, or it breaks the Splatoon reveal. 6) Blue being in two pairs makes per-colour lore messier. The 'perennial finalist' gag covers it, but a fourth pair would strain it. 7) The candidate/election framing could drift towards real politics. Keep it to swatches and slogans about grass and the Sun, never parties or ballots that look like real ones. Religion is gone, which removes the earlier satire risk, so the 'Feed the Hues' petty-gods hybrid should not bring it back. 8) Rounding to grey is a soft erasure. It must stay comic and resigned, never framed as death. 9) Some ideas depend on a device: sleep as night, battery, rotation and shake. They must never depict real hardware.

longevity.strongest: The cleanest period-proofing: no program name, no OS, palette called 'the Strip'. The Fridge gallery, the Sun as the King of the Hill arena, an Eraser that rounds paint to grey rather than deleting it, and device events (Low Battery, Rotate) are solid.
longevity.weakest: The thinnest content engine. Candidates and greys are sketched rather than characterised, so it falls back towards the one-joke meta it warns against. The device events quietly bring hardware back in, and it is the least pitchable of the five.

gameplay.strongest: It makes the Sun the King of the Hill arena: standing on the uncoloured Sun means colouring it, which ties the mode's objective to the core feud (Orange's and Yellow's claims to the Sun). The HUD rule is explicit: slot 16 only shivers with both colours and never gives away the lead. 'Custom colours are not remembered' is a clean one-line reset for the rematch. The 'Try these!' two-swatch suggestion explains the paired draw. 'Team hues appear only in paint and on players is now the plot'.
gameplay.weakest: The stakes are thin (getting onto the Fridge versus becoming background). Respawn, 2v2 structure and split screen get little attention. The device-sleep and battery gags pull towards a hardware framing, and the cosy tea tone undercuts competitive hype.

production.strongest: It handles period-piece risk most deliberately: no dates, resolutions, extensions or bit depth, the program is unnamed, and there is never a desktop or taskbar. It also sets the most important production rule for the hidden score: the slot-16 HUD swatch only shivers with both colours and never shows the lead. Lore is light (the candidates are swatches with one-line slogans), so the writing load is small. The Fridge gallery is cheap. 'Custom colours are not remembered' explains the rematch in a single line.
production.weakest: The device events (battery, rotate, shake, sleep) re-anchor the game to a phone or tablet and risk depicting real hardware. Candidate characterisation is thin, so the one-joke risk returns. 'Sketchbox' needs a collision check. Tea and fridge lean cosy-childlike, which can undercut the competitive hype.

variants.name: Save Changes to untitled?
variants.angle: This version makes the creator the main character. He is a kid called matt who signs "by matt (age 7)". He is never seen, only felt through his cursor, his hesitation and his trips to dinner. He keeps hovering over Save and then clicking Cancel, and that habit drives every match, every reveal and every rematch. It also starts a slow mystery: who is matt, and why has he never saved?
variants.logline: The whole world is an unsaved drawing called "untitled". Its palette has one free slot, and matt (age 7) keeps hovering over Save and then losing his nerve. Every time the cursor drifts toward Yes, two colours and the box-heads they dressed race to cover the canvas, because whoever is most present when he finally clicks gets the slot and stays forever.
variants.world: Creation is a file called "untitled" in an invented, crude drawing program known only as SCRIBBLE 16. The game draws it badly by hand: a wobbly title bar, three hand-drawn buttons, nothing traced from any real software. The palette has 16 slots. Black and fourteen greys came with the program, which is why the world is grey with black keylines. Slot 16 is empty, so nothing in the world itself has a colour. Colour exists only as candidates that have been mixed but not kept. The program keeps a candidate only when the file is saved, and the file has never been saved. The creator is matt. He signed the bottom-right corner "by matt (age 7)" with a backwards 'a', and the box-heads read that signature the way sailors read the stars. matt is never shown. The world knows him only by evidence. A huge black arrow cursor sometimes drifts across the sky. A flat grey patch was smeared over something he regretted. Sounds come from beyond the canvas edge: a TV, a dog, and a distant "MATT. TEA. NOW." Every box-head knows the dialog. It has appeared many times: "Save changes to untitled?" with Yes, No and Cancel. matt has always clicked Cancel and gone back to drawing. Everyone fears the middle button, and most box-heads pretend it isn't there.
variants.the_colours: The colours are candidates for slot 16. matt mixed each one in the colour dialog, tried it out, and never committed. They are vain, petty and sure he meant to pick them. BLUE appears in two pairings and has the air of a frontrunner: "Every drawing has a sky. Do the maths." ORANGE is loud and insecure, and insists it is "basically red AND yellow, two for one". PINK is sure it is matt's secret favourite and says he "promised" in a way nobody can check. GREEN is the grass lobby: "You cannot draw outside without me. He LOVES outside." YELLOW points out that every picture by a seven-year-old has a sun in the corner, so it is owed. They behave like candidates for class captain rather than gods. They have no scripture or worship, just badges, slogans and sulking. The judges' "Feed the Hues" hybrid fits here only lightly. Colours may be petty and demand loyalty, but the house rule is a child's rule, not a commandment: "RULE 1: NO DRAWING NEATLY (matt says)".
variants.the_creator: matt, age 7, at the family computer. He is the whole world's weather and its only voter, and he can't make up his mind. Only his attention is shown, as states the world can read. FOCUSED: the cursor is close and the box-heads stand up straighter. DRIFTING: the cursor wiggles in idle circles while he thinks, and the arena gets gusty. CALLED AWAY: "MATT. TEA. NOW." The cursor stops dead and the world exhales. These are the "between matches" times. HOVERING: the cursor slides toward Save, and this is a match. He always says yes to Yes in his head and then wants to add one more thing, which is the rematch. The mystery builds slowly. The signature's age goes up as the player progresses ("age 8", "age 9"...), yet the file stays open. Later arenas are clearly drawn by an older hand: a homework diagram, a skateboard phase, a heart drawn and smeared out. The box-heads begin to notice the cursor moves less often and with more care. The question the world keeps asking is never fully answered: how old is matt now, and why hasn't he ever saved? The latest unlock reads "by matt (age 3?)", with the second digit too faded to read.
variants.who_you_play: You play matt's box-heads, the only person he knows how to draw. The square head was the easiest shape, the two dots and a line are a face, and the flat cap is how he draws hair, since he does not believe in curls. The overalls are the important part. When matt tries a new colour, he fills in the nearest box-head's overalls with the Fill tool to see how it looks. So every box-head in coloured overalls is a test swatch, a living preview of a candidate colour, and so is every player.
variants.why_they_fight: For the box-heads, the stakes are about whether they last, and the game plays that for comedy. A saved file keeps everything in it. When the slot is decided, the winning colour's swatches keep their overalls and become official: "Drawn And Kept". The losing colour is dithered to the nearest grey, and so are its overalls. That does not kill anyone. Grey box-heads join the Background, a cheerful, slightly bored crowd who hold the arena signs, sweep up stray pixels and heckle. Nobody wants to be Background on purpose, because Background people never get coloured in, and in a world matt might save someday, being coloured is the only kind of fame there is. Underneath sits a joke worry no one says out loud: if matt ever clicks the middle button, nobody is kept at all. That is why both teams secretly hope he'll click Yes soon, and also why they're quietly relieved each time he clicks Cancel.
variants.reveal_and_rematch: The score stays hidden all match because the world can't count itself while matt is still drawing. When the timer ends, play freezes and the giant cursor glides in. The crude dialog drops down: "Save changes to untitled?" The cursor hovers over Yes, and a hand-drawn progress bar appears: "COUNTING PIXELS..." It fills unevenly and stalls once at 99%, as kids' computers do. The bar settles which colour fills more of the canvas. The losing paint is dithered to grey one row at a time from the top, its swatches turn grey with it, and they shrug and join the Background. The winner's swatches pose. Then, every time, the cursor slides off Yes and onto Cancel, and a hand-scrawled note appears: "wait. one more thing." The slot is open again and the losers' overalls flood back in their colour. That is the rematch, and it is in the fiction. matt is never done.
variants.pairs_explained: SCRIBBLE 16's colour dialog shows only two custom colours at once, with "Compare" swatches side by side. matt mixes two, can't choose, and lets the canvas decide. That is why colours always come in authored pairs. The pairs are matt's recurring dilemmas. BLUE vs ORANGE is the football kit argument. PINK vs GREEN is "the drawing of mum's garden". BLUE vs YELLOW is "sky or sun, you can only have one, it's a rule now". Blue being in two pairs gives it a running grudge. It has never won both on the same day, and the colour select can wink at that.
variants.weapons: The weapons are matt's tools, used the way a seven-year-old uses them. SPRAYER is the Spray Can, matt's favourite, held down far too long. ROLLER is the Brush with the tip size cranked to the biggest square, "the BIG one". BUCKET is the Fill tool, which floods through any gap in a line, and matt never closes a shape, which is why every arena wall has a leak. MISTER is the Spray Can left on size 1 by accident, flavour text "he didn't notice for an hour". Kill or splat flavour, if wanted: being painted over is being "coloured in by the wrong pen".
arenas: CLOSE QUARTERS: The Corner, where matt always starts a drawing and gives up after three strokes. It is cramped, dense and full of half-shapes.
KING OF THE HILL: The Bit He Coloured In, the one region matt ever properly filled, which he keeps returning to. Holding it is holding his attention.
TURBULENCE: Thinking Wiggles, made where matt circles the mouse while deciding. The cursor's wake is literally the wind.
MOVEMENT COURSE: Name Practice, platforms made of matt's practice signatures, each a little neater. The backwards 'a' gets corrected halfway along.
Mid-Undo, where platforms flicker in and out because matt is holding Undo and can't decide where to stop.
Under the Grey Smear: a later, older arena drawn over something matt painted out. The edges of a heart are still visible. Nobody mentions it.
Homework Diagram: a labelled cross-section of a volcano, age 11 or so, with neat arrows. The box-heads find the neatness unsettling.
variants.menus_and_meta: TITLE: the dialog itself, hand-drawn. "Save changes to untitled?" with three buttons. YES = Play. CANCEL = Options ("not yet"). NO = Quit, and choosing it makes every box-head on screen turn and stare in horror before a crude "are you SURE sure?" confirm. TEAM SELECT: the two-swatch colour dialog, with players walking their box-heads up to be filled in. The bucket pours and the overalls take the colour. RESULTS: the progress bar tally and the Cancel joke, with a per-player "most pixels coloured" stat labelled "matt's favourite (today)". PROGRESSION: the signature's age is the level counter. Each age adds things matt drew that year to the file, such as new arenas, Background crowd doodles and sticker rewards ("GOLD STAR - good drawing! love mum"). ATTENTION as ambient meta: the main menu shows matt's current state. The cursor is idle, or a "brb tea" note is taped over the corner, or after a long session the screen dims as though his monitor is about to sleep. MYSTERY BREADCRUMBS live in loading captions and unlock descriptions, never in cutscenes. That suits a local split-screen game with no story mode. A possible far-end unlock, kept optional: the cursor finally clicks Yes, a new dialog asks "Save as:", and the crude text box types out "COLOUR WARS". The game itself is the save. Then the classic Cancel note: "wait. one more thing." Even here, matt is still not done.
variants.escalation: The joke keeps generating content in several ways. (1) Matt grows up across progression, and each age is a new content drop: the dinosaur phase, the football phase, the homework years, the first pixel-art attempt. Each brings new arenas, new Background doodles and a new tone of handwriting in the captions, so the comedy changes rather than repeating. (2) His attention states give events and modifiers for free: Called Away (no cursor, calm), Thinking Wiggles (wind), Holding Undo (flickering geometry), Monitor Sleeping (arena dims, sudden darkness round). (3) Each colour pair carries a running feud with its own win-record banter, Blue's double grudge included. (4) The Background grows. Every lost match adds grey extras who heckle, start a union and hold signs ("NOBODY COLOURS US IN"). (5) The mystery deepens slowly: the faded age, the smeared heart, a second, neater handwriting appearing once ("matt your tea is cold"), and the question of how long a file can stay open. (6) Seasonal content is matt's drawings for occasions: a birthday card arena, a Christmas card arena, a "get well soon grandad" card kept gentle. Each feels hand-made because it is.
tone_captions: SLOT 16: EMPTY. (matt is thinking.)
RULE 1: NO DRAWING NEATLY (matt says)
The cursor has not moved in four minutes. Somewhere, there is tea.
COUNTING PIXELS... 99%... 99%... 99%...
wait. one more thing.
Background crowd reminder: you are not lesser. You are grey. These are different.
Do not look at the middle button. The middle button is looking at nobody. It is fine.
Signature updated: by matt (age 9). File still not saved.
BLUE would like it on record that it has a sky.
