variants.name_options: Game title: "Colour Wars" still fits, and better than before, since this really is a war over one colour slot. Use "Save Changes to untitled?" as the subtitle or tagline rather than the title. Software name: SCRIBBLE 16, an invented name always written in the author's crude lettering. Alternatives: DOODLEBOX 16 or PAINT POT 16; check that none clashes with a real product. File: "untitled", lower case and never given an extension on screen, so it avoids implying any real format. Creator: matt (age 7), signed. The author is Matt, which makes the late meta beat honest rather than borrowed. If that feels too personal, a neutral swap is "by sam (age 7)". The losers: the Background. The winners: Drawn And Kept. The middle button: the Other Button, never labelled on screen beyond "No".
variants.risks: Here are the risks, stated plainly. (1) Software-likeness is the biggest one. A "Save changes to X?" dialog with Yes/No/Cancel is a generic convention, but a cursor, a title bar and a 16-colour palette together push toward Microsoft Paint on Windows 9x. Every UI piece must be drawn crude and invented. Use no real button order, no real title-bar layout, no Start-menu or taskbar references, and the program is always SCRIBBLE 16. A reviewer should check every screen against this. (2) One-joke meta. "Hover, Cancel, rematch" is great the first ten times and could grate by the hundredth. The growing-matt progression and the attention states exist to vary it, but they need actual content behind them, and that is a real authoring cost. (3) The mystery needs a delivery channel the game lacks. A local split-screen shooter has no story mode, so the slow burn lives only in captions, unlocks and arena art. Players who skip loading screens will never see it, so it has to be an optional bonus, not load-bearing. (4) Sentiment and grimness. A child growing up, a smeared heart, a faded age, cold tea and an open file nobody closes can tip into melancholy or worse (absent parent, abandoned computer, death). Keep every clue warm and mundane: he's busy, he's grown up, he still opens it. Never imply loss, and keep "get well soon grandad" out if it reads sad. (5) The Other Button (No / Don't Save) is existential erasure. It must stay a running gag that nobody will look at, never a threat that happens. (6) Self-indulgence. "matt" may read as an in-joke to outsiders. The neutral-name swap is ready. (7) Nostalgia as a period piece. Avoid dating the software; SCRIBBLE 16 should feel like any family computer, not specifically 1998. (8) Readability in play. A giant cursor crossing the sky during a match competes with paint readability on split screens. Keep it mostly to the reveal, the menus and the Turbulence arena, and keep it black and white so team hues never appear in the world. (9) Blue appears in two pairs, so its "personality" needs to stay one character with one consistent shade, or players will assume a bug. (10) The colours must stay petty candidates, not deities, to avoid real-religion satire. The judges' "Feed the Hues" hybrid is adopted only as tone: vanity, slogans and a child's house rule instead of commandments.

longevity.strongest: The weirdest and most distinctive version. Progression is the creator growing up (age 7, 8, 9...), with a drop of new arenas and handwriting for each age. The creator's attention states give modifiers almost for free. The far-end 'Save as: COLOUR WARS' payoff is memorable.
longevity.weakest: The creator replaces the palette fight as the star. Cancelling every time empties each win of its stakes. The mystery has no way to reach players in a split-screen game, and the smeared heart, growing up and cold tea pull hard toward melancholy. 'matt' risks reading as an in-joke.

gameplay.strongest: Matt's attention states work as mode and event modifiers: Thinking Wiggles as Turbulence wind, Holding Undo as flickering geometry, Monitor Sleeping as a dark round. Pairs as a child's recurring dilemmas ('sky or sun, you can only have one, it's a rule now'). In team select, the bucket pours colour into a player's overalls.
gameplay.weakest: The reveal always ends with Cancel ('wait. one more thing.'), which voids the win every match. That damages the main reason to care and makes the result feel meaningless. A giant cursor drifting across the sky mid-match competes with paint readability on split screens. The mystery has no channel that reaches play.

production.strongest: Its arenas come from a child's habits (Name Practice signatures, Thinking Wiggles as wind, holding Undo), which suit the crude art and are cheap to draw. 'COUNTING PIXELS... 99%' stalling is a good low-cost reveal beat. 'RULE 1: NO DRAWING NEATLY (matt says)' is a child's rule rather than a commandment.
production.weakest: It carries the highest grimness risk: a smeared heart, a faded age, 'get well soon grandad', cold tea and an abandoned family computer all point at loss. It is self-indulgent, using the author's real name. The ageing-matt progression is a large, open-ended content commitment. Clicking Cancel after every reveal and flooding the losers' colour back in undercuts the win payoff every match. Its mystery has no delivery channel in a split-screen game.

bible.name: Save Changes to untitled?
bible.angle: This version keeps the v1 spine: the last free palette slot, the Save reveal and the grey world. It replaces the churches with an election that has no gods. The colours are petty candidates, the greys are candidates who lost, and the box-heads are a decorators' union hired to do the campaigns' painting. The software is invented and drawn freehand, and nothing in it is dated.
bible.logline: The world is an unsaved drawing called untitled, and its palette has one empty slot. Two vain colours hire grey box-head decorators to paint the canvas, because when the Hand finally clicks Save, the colour covering the most of the picture gets the slot for good, and the loser is filed under the nearest grey with everyone else who ever lost.
bible.world:
Creation is one picture, untitled, open in a drawing program that is never named. The drawings just call it the Program. Its windows, buttons and cursor are all drawn badly by the same hand as everything else, so it could be from any decade. The picture has never been saved.

Along the bottom of the sky runs the Strip, a row of sixteen square slots. Slot 1 is Black, the Keyline. Black outlines everything, never stands for election, and is the reason a Fill stops at a wall. Slots 2 to 15 are fourteen greys. Slot 16 is a dashed empty square with a hand-lettered sign on it: VACANT. ENQUIRE WITHIN. No colour has ever been kept, so nothing in the world itself has a colour: not the houses, not the hill the Hand keeps redrawing, and not the Sun. The Sun is a grey circle with eight grey lines and a label reading SUN (COLOUR PENDING). Every candidate has promised it to its supporters.

The art direction comes from inside the fiction. The world is grey because the greys are all that is left. The dark value under the paint is the undercoat, the oldest grey of all, and nobody talks about it. The black keyline is the one colour with a job. A splash of colour on the ground is a campaign promise, not a fact. Electoral law (posted on a grey noticeboard in every arena) says a candidate's colour may appear only on ballots, meaning paint, and on its own workers. That is why every poster and billboard in the backdrop is grey.

The noticeboard has four rules, plus a Rule Zero the union added in crayon:
0. THE HAND DOES NOT DRAW WELL. NEITHER WILL YOU.
1. Every pixel is one ballot.
2. A pixel painted twice counts for the latest coat. There are no spoilt ballots, only overruled ones.
3. Polling day is whenever the Hand clicks Save.
4. No counting until the Save. A picture does not add itself up while it is still being drawn.

The greys live in the backdrop. Each grey slot holds every colour that ever lost close to its shade, so the greys are crowded, cheerful, retired and full of opinions. Grey 9 (formerly Teal, among others) wants a recount. Grey 11 was Beige and lost to apathy. They sit on the balconies of the Grey Hall, a social club with a dartboard, and heckle.
bible.the_colours:
The colours are candidates, not gods. Each is a swatch somebody mixed and never kept. They are vain, petty and certain they deserve slot 16. They have no bodies, because the art rules give them none, so each one has to come across through three things: a slogan, a grey campaign poster, and a one-line concession speech. Each needs a tic that works in five words.

BLUE, the perennial candidate: calm, a little tired, and always technically correct. Blue enters every election, which is why it is on two ballots. It has won more often than anyone and has been remembered by nobody. Slogan: BE REASONABLE.
ORANGE, the hazard: loud, high-visibility, and touchy about the fruit. Slogan: CAUTION: WINNING. Also: THE FRUIT IS NAMED AFTER ME. CHECK THE DATES.
PINK, the main character: dresses for every election as if it were a premiere, and treats losing as a costume change. Slogan: PINK IS NOT A SHADE. PINK IS A DECISION.
GREEN, the grassroots candidate: earnest and patient, with a laminated certificate that reads 100% NOT A MIX. Slogan: THE GRASS REMEMBERS.
YELLOW, the relentlessly sunny one: sure the Sun has already endorsed it, and aggressively cheerful about it. Slogan: VOTE BRIGHT. OR ELSE :)

THE GREYS are the chorus: retired losers who are not dead, just demoted to shading. Each kept one habit from its campaign days. Grey 4 (ex-Purple) is still regal about being a shadow.

BLACK, the Keyline, is the only colour with a job. It never campaigns and never speaks, and every candidate both resents it and needs it.
bible.the_creator: The Hand owns the file, and it does not know any of this is going on. It is not a god, a judge or a parent. It is somebody idly doodling who will click Save at some unknown moment. It is only ever seen as a crude arrow cursor and the occasional shadow. It has three habits the drawings treat as natural law. It cannot draw hands. It always starts in the bottom-left corner and gives up halfway. It never names anything, so every file is untitled. It gets called away for tea a lot. Every candidate claims the Hand is on its side, with no evidence at all (THE HAND MOVED SLIGHTLY TOWARDS US). The Hand appears in person only at the Save.
bible.who_you_play:
You play a box-head decorator. The Hand cannot draw hands, so it drew a roller into the first person's fist to hide the fingers, and once you are holding a roller you are a decorator. Everyone it draws looks the same: a square head, two dots, a line for a mouth, a flat stroke on top that is how the Hand draws hair (the drawings agree to call it a cap), and overalls, because overalls are one shape and legs are two. The overalls are the only part of a person the Hand ever filled in, so they are the only place a candidate's colour can be worn.

Decorators belong to a union, Local 16, the Amalgamated Society of Grey Decorators. Each election, both candidates hire a crew from the union, because nobody else in the picture owns a roller. Signing on with a candidate means getting its colour put on your overalls. A team of two is a crew, and a four-player match is two firms on the same job. They are rivals, not enemies, and they drink in the same pub.
bible.why_they_fight:
The candidates are fighting for permanence: one slot, kept for good.

The decorators want something more selfish. The Hand can only fill a person in with a colour that is in the palette. When the picture is saved, the winning colour goes into slot 16, and the Hand Fills each winning decorator in properly: a whole person in one colour, not just a coloured work uniform. Every box-head wants to know what they look like coloured in. The losing crew's overalls dither to the nearest grey. Nobody is erased. They go back to how they were, with a sulk.

There is also trade pride. A clean wall, a full fill and nothing missed. Painting over the other crew's work is professional rivalry, and the later coat overrules.

The score is hidden for two reasons. Rule 4 makes counting before the Save illegal (exit polls are banned, and a guilty-looking pollster with a clipboard lurks in the backdrop). And you cannot see a picture from inside it. Each crew can see the paint nearby, but only the Hand sees the whole canvas, and the Hand does not add anything up until it saves.
bible.reveal_and_rematch:
REVEAL (polling day): the clock runs out and everything freezes mid-splat. The Hand's arrow drifts in. A wobbly box is drawn on screen one stroke at a time: 'Save changes to untitled?' The buttons are hand-drawn and deliberately not any real layout: a big YES, a small no, and a third button scribbled out. The arrow hovers over the small no for one awful beat, then clicks YES.

The Returning Officer slides in. It is the progress bar: a long grey rectangle with a box-head face, lying on its side. It is fussy, neutral and nervous. 'I, THE PROGRESS BAR, DO HEREBY BEGIN COUNTING.' It fills in chunky scribbled blocks while the greys lean forward on their balconies. It stalls at 99%... 99%... and then finishes. If the margin is narrow, it announces 'A RECOUNT HAS BEEN REQUESTED. (BY ME. I AM NERVOUS.)', empties, and refills faster. The result does not change; the recount is only there for tension.

The loser gets one concession line in its own colour ('I'd like to thank the grass.' / 'THIS IS A HAZARD.' / 'Darling, I'll be back in a better outfit.'). Then it dithers to grey one row at a time from the top, crossing its own crew's overalls last. The winner flies up into slot 16, the sign flips to OCCUPIED, and the Hand picks up the Fill and clicks each winning decorator so the colour pours in like a bath. The winner starts a victory speech that runs too long, and the Hand cuts it off by moving on.

On an exact tie (a hung canvas), the Hand flips a coin.

REMATCH: the saved picture goes into the Frame, a gallery of every saved picture, where its winner keeps the slot for good. Then the Hand clicks New. The Program does not remember custom colours, so the new file opens with slot 16 vacant and everything grey. The Hand can only draw one kind of person, so it draws the same crew again in the corner, grey and holding tools. The file counter ticks up: untitled (2), untitled (3), untitled (48). Each saved win is permanent, but only in its own picture, so the election happens again every time.
bible.pairs_explained:
The ballot has room for two names, so every election is a two-way race, and each authored pair is a long-running feud with a name.
BLUE vs ORANGE, 'The Old Feud': opposites on the wheel, each sure the other exists to make it look good. Orange shouts and Blue writes 'noted'.
PINK vs GREEN, 'The Garden Party': one flowerbed, two claims. Pink says flowers are the point and Green says the garden is the leaves. Each of these arenas gets one grey flower that both sides claim.
BLUE vs YELLOW, 'The Custody Battle', also known as Sky vs Sun: allegedly Green's parents, running against each other while Green refuses to endorse either ('I am NOT a mix').
Blue is on two ballots because Blue enters every election (it has been provisionally assigned Grey 17, just in case). The random draw at the start of a match is shown as 'NOMINATIONS HAVE CLOSED.' A new pair must arrive with a grudge, not just a balance number. Writing the feud is part of adding the pair.
bible.weapons:
Every weapon is a tool from the Program's toolbar, drawn as a crude icon and carried as union kit. They all exist because something has to hide a hand.
SPRAYER = the Speckle Can, the spray tool. Fast, fizzy coverage. Old hands call it cheating and use it whenever nobody is looking.
ROLLER = the Fat Brush, the widest square brush tip, carried like a broom. The trade says 'You can't fake a roller line.'
BUCKET = the Fill. It floods any enclosed shape, stops only at the Keyline, and leaks through any gap. That is why the union's Rule One is CLOSE YOUR LINES, and why box-heads check their own outlines nervously after a big pour.
MISTER = the Rumour, the smallest spray nozzle. 'A rumour of colour. Rumours count.' Apprentices are given it on their first day and told it is a promotion.
Future tools get the same trade treatment. The Eraser doesn't delete; it rounds paint back to grey, and the union has banned it as contraband. The Line tool is a chalk-line snapper. Nobody touches the Pencil, because it is what the Hand drew them with and using it feels rude.
When you are splatted, you are 'sent back to the yard': redrawn at the site hut in the corner where the Hand always starts, slightly wobblier, with the kettle on.
arenas: The Corner (Close Quarters): the bottom-left of the canvas, where the Hand always starts and always gives up. Cramped, half finished and full of abandoned first strokes. The union's site hut is here.

The Sun (King of the Hill): the grey circle at the top of the sky. Standing on it means colouring the Sun, and every candidate takes that personally. It is reverted to grey after every match, as COLOUR PENDING requires.
The Wobble (Turbulence): drawn while the Hand was shaky. Lines jitter, platforms lurch and paint drifts, and each campaign blames the other.
Warm-Up Scribbles (Movement Course): the loops, zigzags and spirals the Hand does to test the pen. The apprentices train here and the greys hold time trials.
Mid-Undo: somebody is holding the undo key and parts of the arena blink in and out. No candidate admits to wanting anything undone.
The Attempted Horse: an arena inside the Hand's fourth go at a horse. Nobody is sure which end is which, and both ends have a ramp.
800%: the picture zoomed in, where each pixel is a block you can stand on and a single dot from the Rumour is a wall.
Behind the Box: the strip of canvas the Save box always covers. Nobody has ever painted it, and the crews suspect it matters most.
Boundary Review: walls that the Hand's wobbly line tool redraws mid-match, so a gap can open and let a Fill through.
bible.menus_and_meta:
TITLE: a hand-drawn box reads 'COLOUR WARS: Save changes to untitled?' YES plays and the small no opens options ('not yet'). Picking the scribbled-out third button quits: every box-head on screen turns and stares in horror, and an 'are you SURE sure?' box follows. The empty slot 16 blinks in the Strip below.
TEAM SELECT, THE YARD: the random pair is announced ('NOMINATIONS HAVE CLOSED. THE GARDEN PARTY.') with both grey campaign posters. Players walk their box-head up to a candidate's tin, and the Fill pours that colour into their overalls.
STAGE SELECT: thumbnails of parts of the same picture, as if the Hand had scrolled around it.
HUD: the Strip, with slot 16 shivering between both colours. It never shows who is ahead. There are no polling captions.
PAUSE: 'The Hand has gone to make a cup of tea.'
RESULTS: the Save sequence, followed by the Returning Officer's official returns with per-player awards: Most Ballots Cast (most paint), Most Rivals Sent to the Yard, and Quietest Campaign (the mister). Each winning box-head gets a one-line filled-in card ('SLATE: cheeks confirmed.'). The buttons are NEW PICTURE (rematch) and LEAVE THE CANVAS.
PROGRESSION: the Frame is a gallery of the real final canvases, saved as untitled (n). It costs little because the paint map already exists, and every picture in it was made by the players. Further unlocks are Grey Hall portraits, one line each ('Grey 6, formerly Lavender. Lost to Beige. Still not over it.'), toolbar tools, things the Hand attempts to draw (arenas), and cap stickers. All of these are lore and cosmetics, never power.
bible.escalation:
1. Every loss adds to the cast. The greys are the content pipeline. Each lost election files another former candidate under a grey, which gives a new heckler, a new portrait and a new grudge.
2. Every new pair is a writing prompt: a slogan, a poster, two attack lines, a concession and a named feud.
3. Every new arena is something else the Hand tries and fails to draw (a bicycle, 'a crowd', and its own hand, a level the crews refuse to enter).
4. Every new tool is a toolbar icon with a trade spin, plus a new union rule for the loading tips.
4. Every new mode is an election rule: a snap election (a short match called when the Hand gets bored), a runoff, a hung canvas, or Coalition, which is refused ('THERE IS ONE SLOT').
6. The Hand's moods become modifiers: Thinking Wiggles (wind), Holding Undo (flicker) and Screen Dimming (a dark round).
7. Long gags that never pay off: the Sun stays COLOUR PENDING forever. Blue's record keeps growing. Somewhere there is a rumoured update to 256 colours, which would make the whole war pointless. The greys and the union oppose it, and it works as a seasonal threat.
8. The Frame remembers across sessions, so posters and captions can refer to streaks ('BLUE: 4 PICTURES. NONE REMEMBERED BY THE PROGRAM.').
tone_captions: SLOT 16: VACANT. ENQUIRE WITHIN.
RULE 4: NO COUNTING UNTIL THE SAVE. EXIT POLLS ARE ILLEGAL. PLEASE STOP ASKING THE POLLSTER.
LOCAL 16, RULE ONE: CLOSE YOUR LINES.
The Hand cannot draw hands. That is why we all hold something.
SUN (COLOUR PENDING)
DECORATOR SENT BACK TO THE YARD. THE KETTLE IS ON.
I, THE PROGRESS BAR, DECLARE ORANGE ELECTED TO SLOT 16. PLEASE REMAIN CALM. I AM 40% CALM.
GREEN WOULD LIKE TO STATE, FOR THE RECORD, THAT GREEN IS NOT A MIX.
GREY 9 (FORMERLY TEAL): "RECOUNT. I'M JUST SAYING."
Back to grey. Not gone. Just grey, with a sulk.
untitled (48). Same crew. Grey again. Tins out.
bible.name_options:
GAME TITLE: keep COLOUR WARS. It fits better than before, because it is now literally a war between colours over one slot. 'Save changes to untitled?' becomes the tagline, the title-screen box and the name of the reveal moment, not the title. A question is hard to say aloud and hard to search for.
PROGRAM: unnamed on screen and called 'the Program' in-world. If a name is ever needed, use an invented one drawn in the author's hand (Daub, Scrawl or Scribble), checked for collisions with real apps. Never Paint, never '.exe', never PAINT16.
FILE: 'untitled', lower case, with no extension, numbered by save: untitled (2), (3)...
PLACES: the Picture or the Canvas (the world), the Strip (the palette), Slot 16 or 'Sixteen', the Frame (saved gallery), the Yard (respawn hut), the Grey Hall (the greys' club).
PEOPLE: box-heads or decorators of Local 16, the Amalgamated Society of Grey Decorators. The colours are the Candidates. The losers are the Greys. Black is the Keyline. The progress bar is the Returning Officer.
Identifiers in the repository are unaffected.
bible.risks:
1. Trade dress: a save prompt, a cursor, a 16-swatch strip and a progress bar together evoke one famous program. Every window must be drawn freehand, with non-standard buttons (YES, a small no, a scribbled-out third), no real title bars, icons, fonts, button order or palette-grid layout, and no OS, desktop or taskbar. Keep 'Keep this one?' as a fallback title for the box.
2. Period piece: no years, resolutions, file extensions or talk of bit depth. Say 'the Strip has sixteen slots'. The '256 colours' gag is the one deliberate exception and stays comic.
3. Real-world satire: no gods, worship, scripture, temples or mausoleums, and no real-party coding. Candidates campaign only on what they are as colours (sky, grass, the Sun, traffic cones). Election vocabulary stays generic: avoid UK-only terms such as by-election and hustings, and do a regional pass on the Blue, Orange and Green readings.
4. Text load: couch players skip text. Each candidate must work from slogan, poster and concession line alone. Comedy lives in the reveal, the menus and backdrop art, and the game must lose nothing if all of it goes unread.
5. Grimness: going grey is a demotion with a sulk, never death. The greys are a cheerful club, and the threat of the picture never being saved is never stated.
6. One-joke risk: the Save is seen every match, so it needs variation (hovering over the small no, the 99% stall, the recount, the coin flip, a rare double-click) or it becomes a skip button.
7. Hidden score: the HUD and captions must never leak who is ahead.
8. Blue in two pairs: the gag will not stretch to a fourth pair that also includes Blue.
9. Colour-blindness: the pink/green pair needs a readability solution that the premise does not provide.
10. Scope: the Grey Hall, portraits, the Frame and the returns are layers added after the core loop and the reveal ship.

open_decisions.question: How much do the colours speak and have personalities?
options: Vain candidates with a slogan, a poster and a one-line concession each (the v2 default)
Mute tins: personality only through the decorators' trade folklore ('Orange shows every mistake')
Full campaign cast: attack ads, internal polling and gossip between pairs
Somewhere between: mute during play, with one line each only at the reveal
open_decisions.recommendation: Slogan, poster and concession line, nothing more. That keeps the fight for the slot between the colours themselves, which is what the author praised, while the writing load stays small and nothing appears mid-match to leak the score.

open_decisions.question: How far should the election register go?
options: Light: a noticeboard of rules, grey posters, the Returning Officer and a recount
Full civic satire: constituencies, by-elections, hustings, boundary review, coalitions
No elections: the slot simply goes to whoever covers most, framed only as a job and the trade
open_decisions.recommendation: Light, plus generic mode names (snap election, hung canvas). The Returning Officer and Rule 4 do the most work for the least cost, and full civic satire brings in real-party readings and UK-only vocabulary.

open_decisions.question: Who are the box-heads?
options: Union decorators of Local 16 hired by the campaigns (tradesmen, the v2 default)
Volunteers and canvassers who signed up for a colour
Test swatches: drawings the Hand filled in to try a colour
open_decisions.recommendation: Union decorators. This uses the author's 'not against painter tradesmen' hint, gives the bucket's leak rule a home ('CLOSE YOUR LINES'), keeps the rivalry friendly, and avoids anything that reads as worship.

open_decisions.question: What does the rematch mean in the fiction?
options: The Hand clicks New: the win is kept in the Frame as untitled (n), and the Program forgets custom colours (the v2 default)
One more stroke after the save: the '*' returns and the button reads DEMAND A RECOUNT
The program closes and reopens: a by-election with slot 16 empty again
The Hand hovers, then clicks Cancel ('wait. one more thing.')
open_decisions.recommendation: New picture. Every win stays permanent in its own saved picture, so the stakes hold, and the Frame gallery becomes progression built from real matches. Avoid the Cancel version, which empties every win of meaning.

open_decisions.question: Who are the greys, and how much of them do players see?
options: Retired losing candidates crowded into the grey slots, heckling from the Grey Hall, with portrait unlocks
Fourteen named grey decorators, each with a dream (Putty, Slate, Fog...)
Anonymous shading: no characters at all
open_decisions.recommendation: Retired candidates. That explains the grey world from inside the fiction, and every lost election adds to the cast. Ship them first as backdrop heckles, and add portraits later.

open_decisions.question: How is the software presented on screen?
options: Never named on screen, every window drawn freehand, the box reads 'Save changes to untitled?' with non-standard buttons
An invented on-screen name (Daub, Scrawl or Scribble) in the author's lettering
Retitle the box to 'Keep this one?' and drop the software wording entirely
open_decisions.recommendation: Unnamed and freehand, with the scribbled-out third button. Keep 'Keep this one?' ready as a fallback if the trade-dress worry ever grows. Check any name before using it.

changes_from_v1: The colours are now petty election candidates rather than two churches of the Left and Right Click. The 'Feed the Hues' hybrid survives only as pettiness. There are no gods, scripture or commandments.

The greys are now former candidates who lost, filed under the nearest grey, retired and heckling. This explains the grey world, the dark undercoat and the keyline from inside the fiction, and gives a cast that grows with every loss.
The palette arithmetic is fixed: black, fourteen greys and an empty slot 16. 'Yellow is taken' is gone, so the blue/yellow pair is a clean contest.
All period and brand markers are removed: no .bmp, no 640x480, no 1998 and no named program. The palette is 'the Strip' and every window is drawn freehand with non-standard buttons.
The box-heads are now tradesman decorators in a union (Local 16), and 'The Hand cannot draw hands, so everyone holds a tool' explains both the trade and the weapons.
The box-heads have their own stake: the Hand Fills the winning crew in properly. Losers go back to grey with a sulk. The v1 version, where losers were simply dithered away, is gone.
The hidden score now rests on Rule 4 (no counting before the Save, exit polls illegal) and on not being able to see a picture from inside it. The HUD swatch never shows the lead.

The reveal gains the Returning Officer progress-bar mascot, the hover over 'no', a stall at 99%, recount theatre on close margins, concession lines, the losing crew greying last, and a coin flip on a hung canvas.
The rematch is now the Hand clicking New: each win is kept for good in the Frame gallery as untitled (n), and the live palette forgets custom colours.
The pairs are now named feuds (The Old Feud, The Garden Party, The Custody Battle), and Blue's presence in two pairs is a joke ('Blue enters every election').
The weapons were renamed as trade kit (the Speckle Can, the Fat Brush, the Fill, the Rumour). The bucket's leak is tied to the union rule CLOSE YOUR LINES, and splats send you back to the Yard.

The arenas are mapped to the existing modes: the Corner for Close Quarters, the Sun for King of the Hill, the Wobble for Turbulence and Warm-Up Scribbles for the Movement Course. The Attempted Horse, Behind the Box and Boundary Review are new.
Colour Wars stays the title, with 'Save changes to untitled?' as the tagline and the name of the reveal.

judge_notes.longevity: Under this lens palette-gods wins clearly, because it alone turns the art direction itself (a grey world) into a growing cast. Every lost election makes another grey character, so the content pipeline writes itself and the slot fight stays at the centre. Recommended spine: palette-gods' candidates and retired greys, framed as politics rather than divinity as it already does. On top of that, election's Returning Officer as the mascot and menu voice, plus Rule 4/exit polls for the hidden score. From grey-decorators take the palette arithmetic fix, Local 16 / CLOSE YOUR LINES for the Bucket, the 'cannot draw hands' origin, the Frame gallery of real canvases, and the Fill-in victory beat. This also answers the author's 'not against painter tradesmen': box-heads are union decorators hired by the candidates. Keep the Hand an oblivious doodler. The matt-age-7 creator focus and the timeless device events are best mined for modifiers, not adopted as the frame. Reject 'THOU SHALT NOT DRAW WELL' as a commandment and keep it as union Rule Zero. Watch-outs: the gods need non-text expression (poster, slogan and concession line only), the Blue-in-two-pairs gag will not stretch to a fourth pair, and real-politics colour readings need a regional pass.
judge_notes.gameplay: Under the gameplay lens the best spine is the election variant's rules framework: Rule 4 hidden score, overwrite = overruled ballot, HQ respawn, recount, by-election reset, grey posters by law. On top of it, the grey-decorators variant supplies the personal stake and payoff (being coloured in by the Fill), its split-screen honesty and its palette arithmetic. Palette-gods supplies the grey-world lore (greys are past losers) and the pair-feud identity. Avoid two traps. The first is matt-age-7's always-Cancel reveal, which voids the win. The second is palette-gods' 'tie means Don't Save' stake, which is confusing and does nothing in play. Any in-match 'polling' caption must be visibly unreliable, or left out, so it never leaks the lead.
judge_notes.production:
Under the production and risk lens the recommended spine is the grey-decorators variant: a tradesman union, mute tins, the 'can't draw hands' explanation, the Fill-in payoff on players and the Frame gallery. Add the timeless variant's anti-period discipline and its rule that the HUD never shows the lead. From the other variants, take only the cheapest set pieces: the Keyline and the grey Sun (palette-gods), the progress-bar Returning Officer and the theatrical recount (election), and the 99% stall (matt).

Do not adopt the judges' 'Feed the Hues' petty-gods hybrid as gods. Every variant that keeps deities or votes trades one real-world satire risk for another: religion for palette-gods, real party politics for election. Colour personality should live in folklore or one-line slogans, not in the cast.

Shared trade-dress caveat: 'Save changes to untitled?' with YES/NO/CANCEL plus a 16-swatch strip plus a cursor still collectively evokes one famous program. Keep the buttons non-standard (YES/NO/UH, or a scribbled-out third button) and hand-drawn. Keep 'Keep this one?' as a fallback.

Grimness watch: greying out must always read as demotion or going back to background, never death. Avoid mausoleums, 'blank before the file', ageing children and smeared hearts.

Scope watch: named greys with dreams, career records and the posters are all deferrable layers on top of the core loop and the reveal.
